articles.title: A pregnant mom let her 5-year-old stay outside to collect goose feathers – and was placed on the child abuse and neglect registry
articles.author: Jennifer L. Brinkley, Assistant Professor of Law, University of Dayton
paras: Ford’s Colony in Williamsburg is a leafy, gated community in Virginia’s colonial-era historic region with 10 miles of trails and 24-hour security.

On June 5, 2026, Karyann Parkinson, a recent law school graduate pregnant with her fifth child, was on a walk through their neighborhood in Ford’s Colony with her 5-year-old son. On their way home, her son asked if he could collect a few goose feathers at a nearby pond. She said yes, confident in his ability to walk there and back safely.

About 20 minutes later, a security guard from Ford’s Colony knocked on her door, with her son by his side. He explained that a neighbor had seen the child walking by himself, and that he was going to call the police to report her. Within an hour, law enforcement and child protective services were at Parkinson’s door to inform her that they were investigating her for neglect.

After being placed on the child abuse and neglect registry for lack of supervision, Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and received a six-month suspended jail sentence. Parkinson has appealed to the Circuit Court and will have a jury trial in 2027.

I stumbled upon Parkinson’s case while researching and writing a law review article about states that are trying to encourage childhood independence by lessening penalties on parents who allow their children to play outdoors while unsupervised. Virginia, ironically, is one of those states.
Parkinson’s experience is not unique. In my scholarship and in my work as a family lawyer, I’ve seen how overly broad child neglect laws can fail families.

These statutes are being revisited as scholars, psychologists and journalists are increasingly finding fault with “helicopter parenting,” or overprotective parenting that limits children’s independence and autonomy.
Yet cases like Parkinson’s suggest that when the boundaries of neglect are unclear, the law continues to give parents a powerful incentive to err on the side of constant supervision.
Vague language casts a wide net
In 1974, Congress passed the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act to promote child safety and improve how child welfare services are provided.
The law provides federal funding to states to improve child protective services systems. It also requires states to have procedures for reporting instances of child abuse and neglect.
To obtain federal funding, states must comply with certain investigative procedures and reporting guidelines.
However, states enact their own laws on child abuse and neglect, each of which includes its own definitions and procedures, such as determining who must report suspected abuse or neglect.

In an effort to ensure instances of true neglect don’t fall through the cracks, state laws typically use vague language. Tennessee, for example, describes a neglected child as “under unlawful or improper care,” while Mississippi law categorizes a child as neglected if they are without “proper care, custody, supervision, or support.”

This is how a child whose mom has determined he’s mature enough to collect goose feathers on his own ends up being drawn into the system: An agency could argue that she wasn’t properly supervising him.
The Parkinson family is not alone
Other investigations of mothers for child neglect under similar circumstances have regularly cropped up over the past 20 years.

In 2013, an Illinois mother named Natasha Felix let her 11-, 9- and 5-year-old children play in the park adjacent to their home. Even though she could see them from the window, the state determined she met the definition of neglect due to inadequate supervision, a finding that was later reversed.

In 2014, a South Carolina mother, Debra Harrell, was working at a McDonald’s while her daughter was on summer vacation. During her shift, she allowed her 9-year-old daughter to play at a park about a mile away, giving her a cellphone in case she needed to get in touch. Harrell was arrested for felony child neglect, spent 17 days in jail and temporarily lost custody of her daughter.

A Georgia mother, Brittany Patterson, was investigated in 2024 because her 10-year-old son had taken a walk to a scenic mountain hamlet called Mineral Bluff, which was about a mile from his home. A woman saw him walking on the road and called the police. Law enforcement arrested the mother for reckless conduct. The charges were ultimately dismissed in 2025.
Laws may encourage parents to be overprotective, but parenting research is recommending the opposite.

A 2020 study found that kids set free to roam on their own feel more confident navigating new places in adulthood. And other research has found that permissive parenting styles – the kind that can give kids opportunities to take risks, whether it’s climbing a tall structure on the playground or exploring the woods behind their house – help kids learn how to tolerate failure, distress and uncertainty, and ultimately develop into more competent adults.

That may explain why, in 2018, Utah amended its neglect statute to permit children to engage in independent activities like walking to school or playing outside, becoming the first state to do so. Since then, 12 states have amended neglect statutes to recognize childhood independence, including Georgia. After media coverage of Patterson’s case, Georgia lawmakers revised the legal definition of neglect to allow children of sufficient maturity and ability to engage in independent activities, such as playing outdoors or running errands to a convenience store. The definition further added that neglect should involve blatant disregard of parental responsibilities resulting in a real, significant and imminent risk of harm to the child.
Yet despite these efforts, parents continue to be punished for the decisions they’ve made when no harm was inflicted on the child.

A finding of neglect carries serious consequences. It can impact a parent’s future employment and can result in a child’s removal from the home. Concurrent criminal charges can carry penalties of imprisonment, fines and other conditions like attending parenting classes and mandated compliance with child protective services directives. Since mothers are more likely to be the primary caregiver, they face increased exposure and scrutiny under these laws.
Weighing safety against parental rights

The Virginia General Assembly also amended its child neglect definition in 2023 to clarify that children could engage in independent activities without adult supervision, like playing outdoors or traveling to nearby locations on foot or bicycle. It stipulated that activities simply needed to be age-appropriate and the child would not be endangered, but it didn’t define a minimum age for when children could be unsupervised.
In other words, the Legislature left it to parents to determine when their child would be mature enough to participate in unsupervised activities.
So how did Karyann Parkinson, who had no history of abuse or neglect, still get caught up in the system?

In the police report, the officer noted that the 5-year-old was walking unattended about a half-mile from his home, in close proximity to a pond. The officer also added that Parkinson “demonstrated no remorse” and that she believed her son was mature enough to walk there and back for the feathers.

Parkinson has argued that she decided to allow her son to collect feathers on his own to instill confidence in him, not to put him at risk. Her son had been placed in swimming lessons to ensure he would be safe around bodies of water.

Police officers, social workers and prosecutors all share a fear of overlooking abuse or harm. And to be sure, this has also happened: In 2025, a 32-year-old Connecticut man set fire to a home where he was allegedly being held captive for over two decades. Ensuing reporting found that child protection authorities had failed to identify and stop the alleged abuse in the years prior, despite repeated concerns raised by teachers and schoolmates.

When serious cases like this one come to light, the resulting media scrutiny can expose agencies to public criticism and cost state workers their jobs. This scrutiny can create incentives for law enforcement and child welfare agencies to investigate cases thoroughly.
At the same time, it can also foster a culture of overreaction.

A commonsense approach to child protection balances safety with knowledge of the specific child and parents involved. And I don’t think it’s in a state’s interest to have frivolous cases consume limited resources, particularly given the high turnover and heavy workloads in child protective services.

articles.title: Rabbits were a medieval royal luxury in England – until the Black Death made them commonplace
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species.

The early history of rabbits in the British Isles tells the captivating story of social change in medieval England. From a rare luxury gifted by kings and the Norman aristocracy, rabbits became more commonplace after the living standards of the poor improved in the years after the Black Death (1346 to 1353).
The satirical depictions of rabbits found in medieval books reveal a gallows humour for social inversion that would not feel out of place today.

Once thought to have been introduced by the Normans, archaeologists have since uncovered a rabbit bone from Roman Britain. However, documentary evidence of rabbits in the British Isles has only been found from the Norman period onwards.

One of the earliest references survives from the Scilly Isles in the form of a tithe, which was a tenth of produce given to the church as an offering. In 1176, the landowner Richard de Wyka admitted that he had withheld paying tithes on his rabbits because he had believed that “tithes were not payable on things of this kind”. His confusion suggests that rabbits were a novelty.

Rabbits continued to be sufficiently rare to warrant the king’s care and attention in the 1200s. In 1235, Henry III gave a gift of ten live rabbits to Geoffrey Despenser, the English landowner and Lord of Martley in Worcestershire, out of his park at Guildford.

A few years later, the king sent men to catch 30 or 40 rabbits in his Guildford park. They were told only to collect them if the warren was well stocked, indicating that the king didn’t want the colony to be depleted.

At the time, rabbits were kept for their meat and fur. Henry III sent out orders for the supply of venison, boars, fish, swans, peacocks, hens, eggs, and hares for various feasts in the early 13th century. It had not been until his Christmas feast of 1240 that he added rabbits to his requisition list.

Rabbits were an expensive delicacy, costing four or five times as much as chickens. Their owners guarded their warrens against poaching and predators to the point that watchtowers and stone lodges were built to protect them.

Yet rabbits did not remain the preserve of the aristocracy. The Black Death (1346 to 1353), which killed between a third and two-thirds of the European population, led to improving living standards for the survivors. Land became more freely available. Labourers could also charge more for their work. And many adopted the lifestyles of those higher up the social ladder.

Legislation was introduced in 1363 to restrict what people could wear according to their social status. Its introduction was explained because of “the excess of dress of people beyond their estate, to the very great destruction and impoverishment of the land.”
Rabbits reflected this social change. They became more commonplace during the 14th and 15th centuries as their meat was eaten by wealthier peasants and their furs worn by aspiring craftsmen.

The fur of the common grey rabbit was used for warmth, but some warrens specialised in rarer silver-grey or black rabbits. Rabbits were still fit for a king and Henry VII had night attire tailored with black rabbit fur.

As rabbit numbers increased through breeding, so too did the number of complaints about the destruction caused by them. Manorial accounts included repeated protests about the loss of crops and damage to land caused by the lord’s rabbits.

At the same time, hunting rabbits and other game was seen as potentially subversive. In 1390, following the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, parliament introduced legislation against poaching and hunting by labourers and artisans. It was feared that, under the guise of hunting, such people would “make plots and conspiracies of rebellion” against the king.

The king consented to the legislation, extending the ban to the use of “hounds and ferrets, hays, nets, hair-pipes, cords and all other devices to take or destroy beasts of the forest, hares or rabbits, or other sport of gentlefolk”.

Rabbits and hares also reveal the satirical humour of medieval society. The Killer Rabbit of Caerbannog, the fictional and deceptively deadly rabbit from Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975), is but a modern adaptation of this ironic imagery associated with medieval rabbits.

Rabbits adorn the margins of medieval manuscripts. Playful portrayals of rabbits jousting on the backs of snails point to a gentle self-mockery that pervades medieval culture – in this case of chivalric ideals. More in line with the killer rabbit myth, some went even further, depicting rabbits as violently attacking people and seeking retribution.

The Smithfield Decretals, a manuscript illuminated in London in the 1340s, contains one of the most elaborate of such examples. In it, rabbits are portrayed as turning the tables on their hunters, capturing them, holding them trial, and then executing their human and greyhound hunters.

Such examples fit well within the medieval culture of inverting society – the world turned upside down – for comedic relief. Similar examples include the practice of electing a boy as the bishop for the day in Durham or electing a “lord of misrule” during May Day games.
By 1555 the Swiss naturalist Conrad Gesner could write that “there are few countries wherein coneys (rabbits) do not breed, but the most plenty of all is in England”.
Alex Brown is currently the Principal Investigator of a Leverhulme Trust funded project on 'Modelling the Black Death'.

articles.title: Prime’s Carrie miniseries expands Stephen King’s story – but weakens its central horror
articles.author: Ahmed Honeini, Honorary Research Associate in American Literature, Royal Holloway, University of London
paras: Warning: this article contains spoilers for those not familiar with the plot of Stephen King’s Carrie.

Amazon Prime’s Carrie is the fourth screen adaptation of Stephen King’s debut novel. Developed by frequent King collaborator Mike Flanagan (who also directed Gerald’s Game, Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck), this eight-episode miniseries follows the legacy of Brian De Palma’s classic 1976 film starring Sissy Spacek.
Published in 1974, King’s original book tells the story of the infamous “black prom” through a tense, tight mix of prose, fake news reports and eyewitness interviews.

Bullied teenager Carrie White, who lives alone with her religious zealot mother in a quiet Maine town, discovers that she has supernatural, telekinetic powers (the ability to manipulate matter with her mind). After being invited to the senior prom by high school heartthrob Tommy Ross, she finally has a chance to escape her mother’s influence and find acceptance among her peers. But when events at prom take a dramatic, horrific turn, Carrie’s powers are finally unleashed.

In the first few episodes, Flanagan is surprisingly faithful to King’s novel. He also usefully deepens the moral complexity behind much of the story’s events. Chris Hargensen, Carrie’s nemesis, is developed beyond being simply villainous and cold-hearted. Instead, she is shown to be as troubled and afflicted by social and parental pressure as Carrie is herself.

The performances of the central cast are excellent. Summer H. Howell as Carrie, Alison Thornton as Chris and Siena Agudong as their mutual friend Sue Snell are standouts. And Flanagan’s aesthetic flourishes are, at times, masterful. A montage in the penultimate episode set to Lana Del Rey’s song Did You Know There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd showcases the lead-up to and arrival at prom that evokes both adolescent wonderment and anxious dread at the events about to unfold.
However, Flanagan’s expansion of the novel’s events are also this adaptation’s fundamental weaknesses.

The original novel and the classic film adaptation are tightly structured and compact. The Prime mini series, meanwhile, stretches events over the course of eight nearly hour-long episodes. The novel’s brevity – it’s just over 200 pages in most editions – compounds the claustrophobic atmosphere of the intense bullying Carrie suffers, which makes the tragedy of the black prom even more acute.

Crucially, the novel and film also keep Carrie isolated from Chris, Sue and the other girls at school, whereas Flanagan depicts Carrie forming an unlikely friendship with them even after they begin bullying her. This alteration makes little narrative sense especially given that, in the novel, the prom is depicted as the climax of Carrie’s young life and a moment of burgeoning, long-deferred social acceptance.

Flanagan’s major error is in his creation of an entirely new character, Emaline (Thalia Dudek), a fellow telekinetic who negatively influences Carrie’s behaviour. Emaline encourages Carrie to not only hone and strengthen her powers but to strike back at her bullies.

To my mind, this change undermines the entire point of King’s novel and diminishes precisely why the story continues to be so powerful after more than half a century: the black prom is the moment at which Carrie finally exerts agency, control and power over her tormentors. To take that power away from her is a morally neat and misguided attempt at clearing Carrie of wrongdoing. It undermines the implication in the original novel that, perhaps, Carrie’s actions can be understood if not condoned or justified.

In a post-Columbine context where school massacres are common across the US, the implication that Carrie’s actions during the prom could be comprehensible was probably too unpalatable and divisive for the studio.

Carrie shares many similarities with King’s 1977 novel Rage (originally published under his alias, Richard Bachman). It has been permanently taken out of print by King himself after the novel was linked to several real-life high school shootings.

When seen in that context, updating these details of Carrie’s original plot allows Flanagan to approach difficult material with sensitivity. Yet, if the subject matter raises such uncomfortable questions, would viewers not benefit from a new story that, while heavily inspired by King’s original tale, makes its own unique narrative contribution to the horror genre?
Overall, Flanagan’s Carrie fails to satisfy as much as the original novel or 1976 film adaptation do, which is unfortunate, because the series shines when it is most faithful to the source material.

Flanagan shared in an interview that King’s first response to plans for a new adaptation was: “Leave her [Carrie] alone. She’s been through enough.” Carrie, and the audience, may have been better served if Flanagan had taken the author’s advice.

articles.title: The complicated history of women being seen as ‘monstrous bitches’ – from ancient Mesopatamia to modern film
articles.author: Andrea Holck, Lecturer in English Literature and Publishing, City St George's, University of London
paras: It’s news to no one that women have been consistently demonised in popular culture for a very, very long time. In her new book, Monstrous Bitch: A History of Terrifying Women, feminist academic Eleanor Johnson takes us on a detailed and delightfully macabre tour of the history of female monstrosity.

Johnson maps the 4,000-year-old tradition of framing nonconforming women as murderous, monstrous anomalies. Her central argument is that the perennial monstrous bitch, in any of its many forms, is a spectre formed in response to the patriarchy’s fear of women and belief that they’re inherently evil. These women threaten the decency and mild manners of the “good” men and women who uphold the order of the patriarchy.

In Monstrous Bitch: A History of Terrifying Women, Johnson shows us that despite differences in language, region, culture and time period, the monstrous bitch’s fundamental nature, purpose and even origin remain surprisingly consistent. This is because the patriarchy has remained consistent. This is an observation that is far less surprising, particularly in our current moment, as we witness a devastating rollback of women’s rights around the globe.
Johnson takes us through eight major historical phases of monstrous bitchery, beginning with the demonesses of ancient Mesopotamia, who were terrifying she-dogs.

From there, Johnson introduces us to the witches of ancient Greece whose horrific acts of infanticide directly echo those of their ancient forebears. For instance, Medea becomes the inheritor of the likes of Lamashtu, who was the Mesopotamian demoness of infanticide and is frequently depicted as having a hairy human body and the head of a lioness or a dog. In Medea’s case, she intentionally killed her sons as the ultimate act of revenge against her unfaithful husband, Jason. Medea, Johnson notes, is said to come from the east too.

We move through ancient Rome, where monstrous bitches prey on babies and pregnant women. Then on to the whore of Babylon and her many witchy avatars, whose power comes directly from their consort, Satan – patriarchy incarnate.

In each chapter, Johnson gives detailed portraits of these monstrous bitches, drawing primarily on historical texts of their respective times. These women come from the plays of Aeschylus and Euripides, Christian texts, Shakespearean plays, and Romantic poetry, to modern American and European cinema.

One of the book’s most engaging chapters explores vampiresses, who actually do seem like a genuine counter force to patriarchy. They achieved this through their overt sapphic eroticism and nocturnal habit of traipsing about, literally draining the lifeblood out of men and becoming all the more powerful for it.

Johnson argues that these vampiresses, like all the monstrous bitches examined in her book, also descend from an ancient Mesopotamian lineage. However, she does little to support this claim. Though she assures us that the connection stems from the “orientalising fervor” of the Enlightenment period, she supplies little evidence outside of the vague claim that vampiresses are, like the Greek and Roman bitches, said to originate in the east.

Despite the often delicious depictions of feminine monstrosity, the book’s deeper critical arguments remain somewhat underdeveloped. This is particularly true when compared with similar texts such as Barbara Creed’s work on the Monstrous-Feminine (1993) or Carol J. Clover’s many influential feminist critiques of modern horror cinema.

Johnson’s chapter on modern horror cinema, which she pinpoints as the locus of our current era of monstrous bitches, offers some of the book’s most insightful analyses of monstrous bitchery. It’s also where Johnson seems most at home, writing with particular conviction about her favourite feminist films, including Robert Eggers’ The Witch (2015) and Coralie Fargeat’s The Substance (2024).

In her discussion of The Exorcist (1973), for example, we see an intriguing reading of the film as a rare instance of a male character, a priest no less, taking responsibility for a monstrous consequence of patriarchy: a demoness imprisoned in the body of a prepubescent girl. This priest gives his life to save her, in what can be read as a striking feminist twist.

Johnson goes on to describe how at odds the story of the Exorcist is with the circumstances of its making, which involves a misogynistic director torturing the two female leads. This attention to the conditions that give rise to the production of a given film adds depth to the analysis and makes for a more compelling read. Unfortunately, many sections of the book lack this contextual richness, leaving this reader wanting more.

Ultimately, the book reads as a fascinating catalogue of predominantly western instances of monstrous bitchery, with the occasional foray into a deeper cultural or political analysis of the influences that shaped how monstrous bitches have changed over time. In her conclusion, Johnson calls on us to recognise the monstrous bitch, wherever she may appear, as a “paradigm for demonising women”, and, equally, as “an embodiment of infinite suffering”. I only wish these insights had been explored more fully throughout the book.

articles.title: The little-known 14th century battle that has shaped English, Scottish and French relations
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: On October 17, 1346, the battle of Neville’s Cross was fought outside Durham in the north-east of England. It was a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history that led to the capture of King David II of Scotland. Yet few have heard of it.

Other battles are far better known. Those of Stirling Bridge (1297), Falkirk (1298) and Bannockburn (1314) are more famous because of the exploits of William Wallace and Robert the Bruce. Similarly well-known are the successes of Edward III, the Black Prince and Henry V at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415), respectively.
Yet, less than two months after Crécy, a decisive victory was won in northern England. The battle of Neville’s Cross remains one of the least publicly known but decisive battles in English history.

As Edward III gathered a force of 15,000 men to invade France in 1346, King Philip IV of France requested Scottish aid. He wrote to King David in June and again in July: “I implore you to remember our friendship and our treaties and to strike as hard at England as you can.”
With Edward III and most of his nobles in France, Philip reassured David that England was a “defenceless void”. The opportunity was too good to miss.

David duly invaded England with a force of around 12,000 men on October 7. They stormed the Peel of Liddell, took a ransom from Carlisle and sacked Hexham Abbey, before resting outside Durham at Bearpark on October 16.

The English were not, however, caught unawares. Contrary to Philip’s assurances, Edward had not left his northern border undefended. A force of 6,000 men was raised by the northern lords, Henry Percy, Ralph Neville and the Archbishop of York.

Seeking to catch the Scots unawares, they marched towards Bearpark before dawn on October 17. In the morning mists, the English force stumbled upon a Scottish raiding party led by William Douglas. Douglas hastily fled to inform King David that the English had successfully fielded an army against him.

The Anonimalle Chronicle, an anonymous 14th-century account written at St Mary’s Abbey, reported that David arose from his bed irritated and angrily said: “O man, that cannot be, because in England there are no men left but monks and canons, brothers and priests, swineherds and shepherds, cobblers and skinners; but all the knights are with their king overseas.”
The battle of Neville’s Cross

Two contemporary letters by the prior of Durham and Thomas Sampson described how the English army arrived at the battlefield outside Durham at 9am. The two armies proceeded to stare at each other across the moor for the next five hours. Then the English longbowmen opened fire on the Scots at 2pm, and the battle began in earnest. By 5pm, the Scots were routed and fled the field.

Although the ebb and flow of the battle is difficult to reconstruct, historians have suggested that “victory was achieved, not so much by archery, as by the hard work of fighting hand-to-hand in a fierce melee”.

The chronicle of Meaux Abbey, written at the turn of the 15th century, recorded that “because of their exhaustion and the length of the fight, they rested from the fight for a time, leaning on their spears and weapons”. The Anonimalle Chronicle similarly noted that the armies “rested by agreement and then fought again” on several occasions.

Local legend suggests that King David attempted to flee, hiding underneath Aldin Grange bridge. It is said he was captured because the English saw his reflection in the water of the River Browney. However, most contemporary chronicles record the king fighting courageously.

King David was wounded by two arrows. Despite this, the Scotichronicon, a 15th-century Scottish chronicle, reported that King David managed to knock out two of his captor’s teeth before being overwhelmed.

King David’s captor was a relatively humble Northumberland squire – John de Coupland. He was promoted to the rank of knight banneret, the highest position below the titled aristocracy. He also received a very large annuity of £500 per year (equivalent to just over £290,000 in 2017).
Decisive and devastating result
It was a decisive and devastating result. The Scottish force lost up to 2,000 men, while the prior of Durham wrote that “few of us in the said battle were killed”.

Alongside King David, four Scottish earls and over a dozen major barons were captured. The Earl of Menteith, who had previously paid homage and sworn loyalty to Edward III, was hung, drawn and quartered for treason. The list of the dead included the earls of Moray and Strathearn, the marshal, constable, chancellor and chamberlain of Scotland, as well as many barons and knights.

In the following year, the English were able to occupy virtually of all of Scotland south of the Forth and Clyde rivers. It would take decades for the Scots to recover all they had lost. King David himself spent 11 years as an English prisoner before agreeing to pay a large ransom of 100,000 marks for his freedom (equivalent to just over £39 million in 2017).

The battle of Neville’s Cross was most significant because it stopped a series of potential might-have-beens. A Scottish victory would have put pressure on Edward III to lift his siege of Calais and return to England. Instead, the resounding English victory secured Edward’s northern border for the rest of his long reign. This enabled him to raise 30,000 men for the Calais siege; the largest English force assembled during the hundred years war (1337-1453).

Why, then, is the battle not more famous? Unlike Agincourt, it was not immortalised by Shakespeare. Unlike Bannockburn, national identities have not coalesced around it. The battle has not featured in a major cinematic portrayal. It has faded from popular memory in the long and bloody history of Anglo-Scottish warfare.

Although relatively few people today have heard of Neville’s Cross, the events of a few short hours there one October afternoon were of international significance. They came to shape the relations of England, Scotland and France for years to come.
Alex Brown is currently the Principal Investigator of a Leverhulme Trust funded project on 'Modelling the Black Death'.

articles.title: I discovered a Roman fort in Wales – it may hold the key to the ancient Welsh legend of Macsen Wledig
articles.author: Mark Merrony, Supernumerary Fellow, Archaeology, University of Oxford
paras: My recent discovery of a Roman fort and its extraordinary connection with medieval folklore was the fruition of many hours of painstaking research.

This all began in 2002 when I discovered or, more accurately, rediscovered a Roman villa some 30 kilometres to the southwest of Wales. The site was first identified in the early 19th century by Richard Fenton, a local antiquarian. For several reasons, his reliability has been questioned, but mostly because of the perception that the Romans did not reach west Wales was rife in the Regency period and persists to this day.

When my team and I were digging the villa, a local volunteer asked what a Roman site of this status was doing in the middle of nowhere. This was a good question, and I did not know the answer. However, the archaeologist Sir Mortimer Wheeler dug a similar site on the same latitude in 1922, and I reasoned that both sites could lay close to a Roman road. This began a quest to trace a network of routes through west Wales.

A stretch of Roman road was in fact identified by Fenton in the vale of Whitland. This was excavated in 1995, in advance of the construction of a bypass, but I felt that there was more of a network to be discovered. I made breakthrough in 2022. Several other Romano-British sites have been discovered since Wheeler’s day, including a fort at Wiston near Haverfordwest in 2012–2013, and several villas.

Like Fenton, my observations have attracted a good deal of scepticism, but my heart and mind felt that I was making considerable progress tracing the Roman road network from Pembrokeshire east into Carmarthenshire.

My theory received a boost in 2024 with the observation of earthworks suggestive of a Roman auxiliary fort adjacent to an almost certain Roman road near Crymych in north Pembrokeshire. The earthworks had a characteristic playing-card shape like auxiliary forts and was about three hectares in area, which is typical for this type of military installation.

One corner has been destroyed by the construction of a post-medieval settlement (the village of Crymych), which is still inhabited today. The south of the enclosure is intersected by a leat (aqueduct) which enters the site through a masonry channel. Every Roman fort of course needed a water supply. The site lies adjacent to the A478, which runs straight in that area, and many sections further south are similar, but the line is lost in places which is often the case with Roman roads.
It is my belief that it is part of a previously unidentified major arterial Roman road connecting modern Pembrokeshire with Ceredigion to the north.

My hypothesis gained traction with the results of a limited geophysical survey in October 2025, which placed two rectilinear (straight-lined and right-angled) buildings in the right place. Trial excavations followed in March and July 2025 and a steady trickle of finds followed, including coins, a gaming counter, some Roman pottery and a spindle whorl for spinning wool. A more comprehensive evaluation excavation was needed, however, to establish for certain whether the site was a Roman auxiliary fort.
Connections to Welsh mythology

When I discovered the site in 2024, I began to think that it may relate to Cadair Maxen, the camp of the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus (Macsen Wledig in Welsh). He’s mentioned in the Mabinogion (a collection of medieval Welsh stories) in The Tale of Emperor Maxen, also known as The Dream of Macsen Wledig.

This places the late 4th century usurping emperor on the Frenni Fawr, the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which dominates the site a little over three kilometres to the north-east. However, there are no visible remains of a Roman marching camp on the Frenni Fawr where the emperor is said to have visited.

Our breakthrough came in early September with the excavation of five trenches. Three across the suspected principal buildings (the commander’s house headquarters building and granaries); one in the area to the north where a perimeter road would be expected; and another up-slope where the geophysical survey (non-invasive ground scans detecting buried stone structures and drainage ditches beneath the soil) indicated a track.

In the first and second trenches, we identified the bases of floor structures built of clay and packed with the remnants of thin stone blocks. Many of the latter had been disturbed by intermittent ploughing over many decades.

In the second trench there was a diagonal alignment of stones, which indicated a later phase of civilian occupation. We recovered many pottery sherds, particularly in the second trench and found a kiln which yielded many fragments of Roman ceramic tile.

The third trench had a clay floor consistent with Roman granaries. In the fourth trench we unearthed the remnants of the rampart base and a road surface below plough level with rut marks on their expected orientation. The fifth trench did indeed reveal a track. Its date has yet to be established, but we did recover a small number of pottery sherds which are seemingly Roman.

Other new finds from the site include a lead spindle-whorl, an iron stylus for writing documents and letters on wax tablets, a woodworking axe, a gaming counter, a third-century coin and two later fourth century coins.

The collective findings indicate that the site was once a typical timber fort, probably established during the campaign of the governor Sextus Julius Frontinus between AD74 and 78. It does indeed suggest a connection between the camp of Magnus Maximus mentioned in the Mabinogion and the site I first identified in 2024. Magnus Maximus will feature in my forthcoming book, Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus.

The earthworks are still visible today, almost certainly adjacent to a major Roman road, and would have been more conspicuous in the 4th century and listed on official itineraries. The discovery represents an extraordinary fusion between myth and reality and demonstrates that folklore is often underpinned by fact.

articles.title: Night of a Thousand Hells: a subversive, shapeshifting tale of sisterhood, violence and grief
articles.author: Manjeet Ridon, Associate Dean International, Faculty of Arts, Design & Humanities, De Montfort University
paras: Making the longlist this week for the US National Book Award for translated literature, Intan Paramaditha’s Night of a Thousand Hells is a subversive, shape-shifting novel in which family tragedy becomes political reckoning, horror exposes social violence, and familiar stories turn sinister.

Set in Indonesia, the novel opens in the aftermath of a suicide bombing by a radical group targeting places of worship and community groups. Annisa, a young mother and the youngest of three sisters, is dead, leaving her sisters, Muti and Maya, to confront the question that drives the novel: what led Annisa to get on a motorbike with a bomb strapped to her chest and why did she join this radical group intent on killing innocent men, women and children?
The search for answers to these questions takes the sisters into a world where myth and history, the living and the dead, and innocence and culpability are never easily separated.

Paramaditha’s achievement lies in the way she brings Indonesian folklore, Islamic mysticism and contemporary political violence into conversation with the ghostly legacies of western literature. Three familiar stories are particularly important: Shakespeare’s King Lear, the fairy tale of Cinderella, and the storytelling tradition of One Thousand and One Nights. These are not simply literary references; they become frameworks through which the novel questions power, identity and the stories societies choose to believe.
A miniature political world

Family dynamics in the novel evoke King Lear, with its destructive entanglement of parental authority, patriarchy, favouritism and fractured loyalties. The father’s preference for Annisa helps shape the sisters’ unequal positions within the family, leaving Muti and Maya to negotiate the emotional consequences. As in Shakespeare’s tragedy, the household becomes a miniature political world in which love and loyalty are inseparable from power.
Yet Paramaditha refuses to treat family conflict as a private drama alone: the violence embedded in domestic relationships echoes the wider structures of exclusion and authority beyond the home.

It is Cinderella, however, that provides the novel with its most provocative challenge to conventional storytelling. Muti is named the Caretaker, Maya the Traveller and Annisa the Bride, roles that appear to promise familiar fairytale destinies. But Paramaditha shifts our attention away from the favoured heroine towards those relegated to the margins.

“Revolutions always begin with ugly stepsisters,” becomes the novel’s radical declaration. The stepsisters are no longer merely jealous obstacles to someone else’s happiness; they are figures who expose the unfair rules governing who deserves love, beauty, recognition and a happy ending. Revolution begins when those assigned lesser roles refuse to accept the story written for them.

With its title, the novel clearly echoes One Thousand and One Nights to introduce yet another dimension: storytelling itself as a means of survival and resistance. Like the narrator Scheherazade, whose tales defer death, Paramaditha’s characters inhabit a world where narratives carry power.

But who controls the story, and whose voice is silenced? This is given focus in the chapter titled “No Shahrazad’s Tale”, suggesting that the absence of a story can be as politically significant as its telling. The novel’s interwoven narratives refuse the reassurance of a single authoritative account.

Indonesian folklore adds a further layer of strangeness. The grandmother’s stories of weretigers and shapeshifters evoke a world in which identities are fluid and appearances deceptive. This supernatural atmosphere does not simply provide horror; it unsettles the boundaries through which society distinguishes the acceptable from the monstrous.

Meanwhile, the bombings of a church, a mosque and an Islamic study group for transgender women expose the deadly consequences of ideological certainty. Religious belief, mysticism and political extremism coexist uneasily, without being reduced to a simplistic explanation of violence.

Rohadi, the servant’s son who was raised with the sisters and regarded as a sibling, reappears in the novel as Rosalinda, a transgender woman, to remember the impact of marginalisation inside and outside the family. Once expelled after being suspected of petty theft, Rosalinda embodies the cost of social rejection. Her later role leading a community group for transgender women offers a different kind of belonging, built not on inherited status but on solidarity.

The novel’s striking red cover and mask-like face is reminiscent of South Asian Kathakali dance performances. With its protruding tongue and tiny house lodged in its throat, it captures the novel’s unsettling theatricality: the domestic world swallowed by myth, and a voice struggling to escape confinement.
By the end of the novel, the sisters’ roles have shifted. Muti becomes the traveller, Maya the family caretaker, and Rosalinda builds a safe place for members of her transgender community.

Their endings resist the neat resolution of a fairy tale. In this dark, inventive novel, the ugly stepsisters do not simply demand a place in the old narrative. They begin the revolution by rewriting it.

articles.title: What’s behind the BBC’s funding crisis? An expert explains
articles.author: Patrick Barwise, Emeritus Professor of Management and Marketing, London Business School
paras: In the run-up to the renewal of the BBC charter in January 2028, the corporation is facing perhaps its greatest ever funding crisis. It is staring down cost hyper-inflation across most programme genres and, unlike online-only streamers such as Netflix, it will still have to fund traditional broadcast networks until at least 2034. And of course, it will also have to pay for new digital services to keep pace with trends, especially among younger audiences.

But the biggest driver of the BBC crisis is the cut in real-terms funding for its national, regional and local UK services. These are the services that largely account for licence payers’ willingness to pay the fee.
The reduction in the real-terms funding of these services has been building up since 2010 and is now deeper than most people realise.

In 2010-11, TV licence fee revenue was £3.1 billion. The cost of collecting the licence fee was £124 million. The BBC also received £579 million of government funding from the Department for Work and Pensions for free TV licences for the over-75s.

So the total public funding from licence fees, after collection costs, and the DWP payment, was £3.5 billion. But not all of this went to the BBC: £80 million was “top-sliced” (or diverted) to meet the final costs of switching from analogue to digital TV.

By 2025-26, licence fee income had grown to £3.9 billion. But government support for free TV licences had been phased out and top-slicing increased to £293 million to fund the BBC World Service, BBC Monitoring (a division of the World Service), and the Local Democracy Reporting Service. The BBC was also partially funding the Welsh language TV channel S4C. That left the net public funding of its UK services at around £3.4 billion.

But between 2010 and 2025, the cumulative effect of inflation was 55.4%. This equates to a real-terms cut to public funding for the UK services of £2 billion per year – or put another way, a 37% drop in income.

Based on media coverage, you might think that the main reason for the BBC’s reduced income is that fewer people are paying the licence fee. But in reality, the 37% real-terms reduction was mainly driven by three other things.

First, successive governments were salami-slicing the value of the licence fee – in other words, repeated below-inflation settlements ate away at its value over time. Second, they withdrew government funding for free TV licences. Third, they more than doubled top-slicing in real terms, from £124 million to £293 million.
How BBC funding has fallen (figures in millions of pounds)

It’s true though that increases in licence fee evasion, from 5.2% in 2010-11 to 11.8% in 2025-26, played a part, as did the number of “no licence needed” households claiming that they did not need a TV licence because they “watch TV only on demand” but “never watch the BBC iPlayer”.

To put this into context, in 2015 99% of UK households used the BBC’s services in a single week. The figure may now be “only” 97% or 98%. But the idea that a large number are forced to pay without getting any direct benefit over a whole year seems implausible.
Many, however, take the BBC for granted – until they’re deprived of it. A study in 2022 found that after nine days without it, 70% of those who’d said it was poor value changed their minds.

To mitigate the cuts, the BBC has made continuous efficiency savings over the 15 years, reducing overhead costs, cutting staff and budgets, and squeezing suppliers. But, according to the National Audit Office, it now faces diminishing returns from these savings and most future cost-cutting will have to come from axed programmes, lower budgets and a reduction in the number of TV channels and radio stations. The axing of long-running Radio 4 consumer show You and Yours – along with other casualties – is a case in point.

The BBC also faces diminishing returns from commercial income, largely raised overseas from programme sales and format licences. With less investment in original content, quite simply the BBC now has less to sell.

The government says it wants to ensure sustainable BBC funding under the next charter. Achieving that will require updating or replacing the licence fee funding model, widening the payment base and bringing it closer to the BBC’s near-universal household usage. The financial stakes are surprisingly low: the £180 licence fee (with easy payment options) is equivalent to just £3.45 per week.

Limited, well-targeted exemptions for households for whom this is still a significant burden should be easily affordable, either for the government or for a properly funded BBC – even in the current fiscal situation. But as always, any policy that ends – or even reverses – the salami-slicing of BBC funding will be strongly opposed by its critics.

articles.title: Her Son’s Wife by Dorothy Canfield Fisher finds profound meaning and emotion in domestic life
articles.author: Katie Harling-Lee, British Academy Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Edinburgh
paras: UK publisher Persephone Books are continuing to reintroduce “lost” 20th century novels by women to the 21st century, featuring what they term “domestic feminism”.
Coined by Persephone founder Nicola Beauman, domestic feminism acknowledges how significant the home is to human life while rejecting the assumption that it “justified a woman’s whole existence”.

In her 1983 book A Very Great Profession: The Woman’s Novel 1914-39, Beauman wrote about how these novels often chronicle “the drama of the undramatic” and “the steadfast dailiness of a life that brings its own rewards”. Persephone’s latest publication is no exception.

Her Son’s Wife by Dorothy Canfield Fisher (1926; republished 2026) tells the story of Mrs Mary Bascomb, a hardworking widow whose life is turned upside down when her son, Ralph, unexpectedly returns home from college with a new wife, Lottie. As the young couple move into Mary’s home and take over the careful domestic sphere she has kept clean and ordered for years, she struggles to defend her space from the changes.

Canfield Fisher was a bestselling and well reviewed American author in the first half of the 20th century. In fact, Her Son’s Wife was tipped to win the Pulitzer prize when it was first published in 1926.

Today, she is no longer a household name and her novels are mostly out of print. In recent years, however, the work of a few publishers has seen some of her books resurfaced. Persephone, for instance, has also re-published her novels The Home-Maker (1924; republished 1999) and The Deepening Stream (1930; republished 2021).

Canfield Fisher lived a full and busy life supporting social reform and education causes alongside writing numerous books. She influenced her contemporary literary scene both through personal relationships with well-known authors, including Willa Cather and Robert Frost, and serving on the selection committee for the Book of the Month Club for 25 years. A book subscription service with a million members by 1950, Canfield Fisher was the only woman on the selection committee at its founding in 1926 where she helped decide what to recommend to the American reading public.

In that same year, Her Son’s Wife was published by Harcourt and Brace publishers and serialised in the American magazine Woman’s Home Companion. Canfield Fisher wrote the majority of this book between 1924 and 1925 at the age of 45, the same age as the novel’s protagonist. She described the plot as revolving around the moment “a woman of 45 meets calamity”, an age when, it is assumed, “most people are set for life”.
Writing Her Son’s Wife was so emotionally draining for Canfield Fisher that she often feared she wouldn’t be able to finish it.
In one letter to her publisher, she described the experience as akin to a terrifying “hallucination”.
These intense emotions are communicated to readers in evocative passages, such as when Mary represses her deep grief for her husband by focusing on everyday housekeeping tasks:

…she was terrified by it as a timid swimmer is panic-struck to feel deep water under him. To what, away from her traditional moorings, would it sweep her, if she let it have its way with her? By long practice she had learnt how to escape from it, filling her mind and hands with little material processes.

There are also moments when Canfield Fisher connects our everyday world with something more profound. Early on in Her Son’s Wife, Mary goes to check her mailbox and steps out “from the box-like walls of her house into infinity. Over her head the sky rose, boundless and black”. A few lines later, the scene is rendered as simply “a dark night in April”, but the mystical and unnerving glimpse of infinite blackness remains.

In my own research into the influence of religion, Quaker silence, and spiritualism on Canfield Fisher’s writing, scenes like these are examples of how she wrote novels about domestic daily life to dive into the profound experiences of human existence. While hesitant to call herself a Quaker outright, Canfield Fisher married into a Quaker family in 1907, became a member of an informal Quaker Meeting in Vermont by 1949, and felt deeply drawn towards the spiritual silence of Quaker Meetings for Worship.

Despite the sympathy readers may feel for grief-stricken Mary, she can be a rather self-righteous character. Watching her new daughter-in-law, Lottie, through Mary’s eyes we may share her frustration at the mess the house is left in; at Lottie’s obsession with looks over substance; and at her dismissal of Mary in all that she has given her (including a house to live in). But we also wonder at the life Lottie has come from to be where she is now, sobbing out the lines:
It’s too mean. I don’t want anything bad. I just want to have things nice, the way anybody does. And you jump on me for it.

In Her Son’s Wife, Canfield Fisher charts the emotional complexities of her characters with her accomplished, skilled approach that allows us to simultaneously sympathise and get frustrated with Mary, Lottie, and Ralph.

In its deft handling of the nuances of family relationships, mental health, and domestic challenges, the novel speaks to our world today even as it captures a distinct moment in time set one hundred years ago. It is a Persephone novel of the highest calibre, and I am excited to see how readers respond to this latest resurfacing of a neglected Canfield Fisher classic.

Katie Harling-Lee receives funding from the British Academy for a postdoctoral fellowship project researching Quaker silence in the novels of Dorothy Canfield Fisher. She has previously worked with Persephone Books to speak about Canfield Fisher's novel The Deepening Stream at the 2024 Persephone Festival.

articles.title: Winter of the Crow: this taut escape thriller explores life under martial law in cold war Poland
articles.author: Sam Edwards, Reader in Modern Political History, Loughborough University
paras: It’s surely no surprise that amid today’s geopolitical turmoil, filmmakers are turning to the events of the cold war for inspiration. A flurry of productions set in the 1980s have been released just this year.

See, for instance, The Brink of War, a political drama focused on the 1986 summit at Reykjavik between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev. Then there’s action-comedy Mayday, starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh. Polish director Kasia Adamik’s new film, Winter of the Crow, is a welcome addition to this burgeoning genre. It’s an evocative film which skilfully exposes the stifling controls and murderous repression inherent in Soviet-era totalitarianism.

Based on a short story by Nobel prize-winning Polish author Olga Tokarczuk and set in December 1981, the film stars the always excellent Lesley Manville as Professor Joan Andrews. She’s a rather blunt British academic invited to give a guest lecture on the other side of the iron curtain, in Warsaw.

The film begins in a world in which Joan is firmly in control – her office in the ivory towers of academia – before shifting to one which is alien and disorientating. The Poland of the 1980s is depicted as a cold, austere and unforgiving place. Joan arrives in a landscape of concrete, blizzards and leaden skies.

After being met at the airport by a young Polish PhD student named Alina (brilliantly played by Zofia Wichlacz) Joan is taken to a university lecture theatre, only to have her talk ambushed by student protesters who are keen to exploit the presence of the press. Joan, ignorant of the severe hardships Poles are enduring, is livid. She is initially indifferent to the students’ cause, believing their fight is not hers. By the following morning, however, the reality of life in the Eastern Bloc becomes all too apparent.

Overnight, in response to growing social unrest linked to a severe economic recession, the Polish government declares martial law. Phone lines are cut, the border is closed and for Joan, trapped in a place that she does not understand, the situation quickly escalates.

She witnesses the heavy-handed arrest of a young mother and then, soon after, sees Alina’s idealist brother, Marek (Jakub Guszkowski), murdered by the secret police (known colloquially as “crows”). What follows is a taut and tense escape thriller in which Joan, Polaroid camera in hand, is pursued through the Warsaw winter by the shadowy agents of the Polish state. Her objective is the safety of the British Embassy and, ultimately, a flight home.

The film is structured around two carefully calibrated parallels. The first is between east and west. The latter is depicted as clean and colourful – a place of red buses and of colleges built of warm sandstone. Glimpsed at the very start, it offers a powerful contrast to the grey monotone of Warsaw.

The second parallel, which Adamik teases out with real skill, concerns the links between Joan’s expertise in psychiatry and the totalitarian police state. It is explored at various points: in the architecture of Warsaw (all those oppressive and state-built tower blocs), in the arresting irony of where Alina seeks refuge at the film’s end (which I won’t spoil here) and in pointed references to the cold war geopolitical context itself.

Early scenes even show a British television journalist explaining the meaning of M.A.D. (Mutually Assured Destruction, the cold war nuclear doctrine). The underlying point is clear. The totalitarian police state is a place of hope-suffocating confinement, much like an asylum.

It is also for this very reason though that Joan proves especially well-equipped to find her way to safety. After all, she is an internationally renowned psychiatrist and so understands landscapes of fear and paranoia far better than most. And she has also spent a career successfully navigating life in British academia, an environment often satirised in the 1980s campus novels of authors like David Lodge for its Machiavellian intrigue, rivalries and betrayals.
For Joan, therefore, outwitting professional spies – however cunning and brutal they might be – is relative child’s play.

Amid heightened east-west tensions provoked by the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, this is a powerful film for its moment, one which brilliantly uncovers the soul-crushing tyranny of life in an Orwellian police state.

In doing so, it also offers a clear takeaway. For as Joan comes to learn firsthand during the cold winter of December 1981, when it comes to the fight against oppression – and for the right to hope and dream – there can be no bystanders.

articles.title: Can AI help ‘humanise’ museums? New report reminds us why art matters in a changing world
articles.author: Sarah Cook, Professor of Museum Studies, University of Glasgow
paras: The cover of a new report on AI from a US museum thinktank restyles the Sistine Chapel’s Creation of Adam, with the hand of God replaced by a Terminator-style robotic one. So far so obvious.
In Remuseum’s Five Ways AI Can Humanise Museums, AI has presumably replaced God as the enabler of all things. But who is Adam’s hand supposed to represent: the museum visitor or the museum worker?

Or could it be the figure of the artist, being granted the power to create new worlds with AI? Creating worlds is exactly what artists can do, and paying attention to their creative and critical uses of AI is an urgent task for art museums today.
This article is part of our State of the Arts series. These articles tackle the challenges of the arts and heritage industry – and celebrate the wins, too.

Written by Remuseum’s founding director Stephen Reily, the report deftly introduces, by way of case studies from seven major American art museums, different ways in which the adoption of AI systems might enhance what they offer.

From communicating with visitors (many museums now have chatbots) to streamlining curatorial tasks, the report shares knowledge from projects which have used AI to develop marketing programmes, aid in fundraising, build relationships with sponsors, facilitate access to collection records online, train staff in new technology, and offer new means of art interpretation.

As a professor of museum studies, and a longtime curator of art that uses technology as both its medium and subject, my work has increasingly turned to consider AI. The report – which aims to inspire confidence by sharing practical examples – is interesting and useful, but I can’t help feel that it glosses over some of the more complex issues behind such innovations.
Museums in a technological age

It clearly calls out and thus aims to diminish resistance to AI from across the museum sector. “Avoidance is not an option,” the report declares – but much like the graphic on the cover, it risks oversimplifying some issues. There has been decades of research into how museums can better use technology, which suggests any resistance from museum staff to AI might be borne of something other than technophobia.

The report names one possible factor dampening museum workers’ enthusiasm for AI: that it will result in potential museum job losses. It answers this worry about AI taking jobs stating: “The best way to preserve and increase museum employment is to make museums matter to more people.”

While this doesn’t exactly address that concern, it introduces examples of how art museums have used AI to better connect with audiences, with all the tangible benefits that accrue from that increased brand visibility.

Why do museums matter to people, and to whom do they matter exactly? Do they matter to me because they offer cutting-edge exhibitions and events, educational and even life-affirming experiences? Or do they matter to you because they do the difficult work of preserving our cultural heritage, warts and all?

Art museums face a particular challenge, as how and why art matters to people is a much debated question. So knowing who art museums matter to and why, is the first step to developing more connected and personalised experiences for audiences, whether enabled by AI or not.
Using AI art to explain our technological age

I was drawn to the opening case study which talks encouragingly about hosting artists in residence to work with new technologies. One example is the Toledo Museum of Art, which in 2023 exhibited UK-based artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg’s work Machine Auguries, a sound and light installation made with AI (which I first co-commissioned in 2019. Machine Auguries is a simulated dawn chorus of birdsong, inviting reflection on the relationship between technologies and nature.
The report proposes this is a way of increasing the understanding of digital art and the creative potential of technology, which can help make museum staff more open to AI.

Ideally the institution’s staff learn from these new artworks not just because they are made with new technologies such as AI, but because they are also often about new technology and its effects on society. Artists like Ginsberg are building new worlds for visitors to experience.

Such works demonstrate that sometimes an art museum is a place where audiences can encounter not just new technologies as the medium for an artwork, but also, its subject. For AI that means not just a demonstration of what it can do (“this artwork is made with AI”), but an interrogation of how it works (“this artwork is about how AI systems are trained to act on our behalf and how they affect us”).

The art museum then becomes, as I’ve long argued, a place where we all can take the time to think about – and through art, feel – what new technologies might mean for us in our world. This is a crucial way museums might “matter to more people” especially in times of technological change.

Of course questions remain. Who is encouraging art museums to choose AI in their operations, who is benefiting and who is losing out? What constitutes “responsible reuse of a museum’s own assets”? Is my data, as a visitor, such an asset? How do we deploy proprietary technology to make “real” art museum experiences matter to a greater number of visitors, without glossing over the complex stack of ethical and legal concerns that sit behind the rollout of any new technology?
This last question is one the report doesn’t quite get to, focused as it is on offering positive and useful examples of the successful deployment of AI in customer-facing activities.

But maybe we should pause and think about how we feel about the potential trade-offs, such as whose data is being shared, and with whom. Museums might want to do too, when it comes to their use of AI beyond the art they display in their galleries.

articles.title: Can memoirs ever tell the whole truth?
articles.author: Emily Hay, Research Assistant in Scottish Literature, University of Glasgow
paras: In July 2025 a literary scandal erupted when The Observer journalist Chloe Hadjimatheou claimed that Raynor Winn, author of the award-winning memoir The Salt Path, had omitted significant facts and invented key parts of her story. This much-loved account of Winn’s transformative and healing coastal walk with her terminally ill husband after they lost their home, had recently been made into a film.

In her article Hadjimatheou maintained that the details of how Winn and her husband lost their home and the nature of his illness were fabricated. Winn responded with a 2,300-word statement on her website defending her memoir and castigated the claims as “grotesquely unfair” and “highly misleading”.

The scandal stunned the publishing world and readers alike, with commentators arguing that audiences expect a level of truth from works labelled as autobiography or memoir. Though sometimes used interchangeably, there are some key differences between each genre.

Autobiography usually denotes a work which details the whole life or work of a public figure narrated from their point of view. Memoir instead recounts certain specific experiences or interactions from the author’s life, allowing writers to explore and communicate their emotions, experiences and beliefs. Its name is literally derived from the French word mémoire, meaning “memory”.

The problem of truth in this genre is almost constantly in the spotlight. While some memoir controversies have centred on what are alleged to be outright lies – such as the Salt Path – others may reflect the tension between a reader’s expectation of objective “truth” in a work of non-fiction, and how authors themselves actually recall and understand their memories.
Swan Song, Charles Spencer’s memoir of life with his sister Princess Diana, which has been accused of getting key details wrong, is a case in point.

Buckingham Palace responded to Spencer’s claims against the royal family, saying: “His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise.” Our memories are subjective reconstructions of events from our point of view, which means that they may always be open to dispute. Memory retrieval can never be linear, and neither can it ever be objective – all of which affects how memoirs are written and how they’re received.
As we are finding in our ongoing research on life-writing, the relationship between truth and fiction in this kind of writing is more often fraught than not.
Fact, fiction and everything in between

All life-writing depends on memory, yet the process of how memories are recalled rarely features in these debates. Our research is concerned with the relationship between memory and life-writing by Scottish authors, many of whom have experience of the care system. We want to know if there are any typical patterns that these writers follow, and to what extent we can test the active memory retrieval of writers today.

Neuroscientists have shown that memories change with time and frequency of use. Memories are also adaptive, part of a highly reconstructive process where we access the most useful information first, and piece in other details around this.

At the core of our research is a series of workshops in which care-experienced adults get to know the workings of memory and are then invited to try life-writing for themselves. We expect fact, fiction – and everything in between.

We see these issues play out in memoirs by the Scottish authors our study centres around. Dorothy K. Haynes wrote a memoir titled Haste Ye Back, detailing her upbringing at Aberlour Orphanage in the northeast of Scotland from 1929-1933.

While Haynes’ memories of Aberlour are largely happy, a 2019 report for the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry uncovered reports of physical, psychological and sexual abuse from former residents from later periods between between 1930 and 1990. Our memories can be coloured by information learned after the fact. Or, like Haynes, we may have completely different personal experiences from the established narrative – does any of that make one person’s account less true than another?

For other authors, personal experiences form the basis of their fictional works, and this can further blur the boundaries between truth and fiction. Jenni Fagan’s novel, The Panopticon, follows a teenager abused but not broken by the Scottish care system. Ootlin, the memoir she published ten years later, demonstrates just how much of that narrative had been based on her real-life experiences.

In circumstances like these, readers can contrast the novel and the memoir for themselves, but elsewhere this isn’t possible. Jessie Kesson’s novel The White Bird Passes details the protagonist Janie’s poverty-stricken upbringing and experience of being sent to an orphanage in Skene, Aberdeenshire, closely mirroring Kesson’s own childhood.

Kesson herself noted in later interviews that although a work of fiction, the work was “mostly autobiographical”, and that she didn’t want to bore people by covering the same ground in a memoir. Can we read Kesson’s novel as a work of life-writing, even when it’s shelved in the fiction section?

At the opposite end of the spectrum, some authors have experimented with the very form of memoir itself. Janice Galloway has written two works she labels “anti-memoirs” – titled This Is Not About Me, and All Made Up respectively.

The works detail an Ayrshire upbringing and family life which mirror Galloway’s own, but with incisive writing that recalls her command of character and detail from her other works of fiction. As her titles attest, the reader can never rest too comfortably in the knowledge that what they are reading is the unembellished truth.

The genius of Galloway’s work isn’t that she pioneers a blend between memoir and fiction for the first time, but that she lays bare the complex relationship between truth and fiction which is present in all life-writing.

Though it may be going too far to call all memoirs fictional, ultimately, what readers take to be “truth” from a memoir, as for any work of literature, is down to them. We can never truly know how another person experienced or remembers events – and that desire for truths and perspectives other than our own is exactly why the genre of the memoir endures.

articles.title: Cecilia Vicuña’s radical eco-feminist vision comes to London
articles.author: Abby Moore, Postgraduate Researcher in Art History, University of Exeter
paras: Living Threads at Whitechapel Gallery is the first major UK exhibition of eco-feminist activist contemporary artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña.

Born on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, in 1948, Vicuña moved to London to study at the Slade School of Fine Art in 1972. While she was in London, Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende, was violently deposed during the 1973 Chilean military coup. This left Vicuña unable to return home because of the threat of violence or death.

When her UK visa expired in 1975, she went to Bogotá, Colombia, then moved to New York in 1980 where she has remained to the present. It was not until recently that Vicuña’s outstanding contributions have been commercially recognised. She received the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement award at the 59th Venice Biennale in 2022 and won the Icon Artist Gold Medal at Art Basel Miami Beach in 2025.
Her new solo exhibition Living Threads contributes to the long-overdue recognition this engaging and important artist deserves.
A gentle dance with living threads

The “living threads” of the exhibition title tell of Vicuña’s ideas around the vitality and effervescence within fibre-based art practice, as well as the invisible connections and interactions between people and plants, animals and the natural world. These ideas have occupied Vicuña’s creativity since her teenage years and are magnificently displayed at Whitechapel.

Upon entering the first gallery space, visitors are presented with a room-filling vision of Quipu Menstrual 1 (unknotted) (2006-24). Streams of raw wool in deep reds, vibrant oranges and soft pinks hang in structured rows. While some strands drape all the way to the floor, others trail off at barely a third of that length, appearing torn and frayed under their own weight. Through its monumental scale, the work directly challenges western ideals of permanence and memorialisation traditionally found in stone statues and monuments.

While stood immobile in front of this enormous installation, there is subtle yet constant movement where the airflow within the gallery drags across the materials. It causes a gentle sway reminiscent of branches in a breeze.

As visitors move around the vast form of Quipu Menstrual, their presence stirs the raw wool into a gentle dance. This motion creates a deep connection between the viewer and the artwork, entangling human hair and airborne fibres with the physical piece. Through these subtle interactions, the porous, shifting material transforms the viewer into an active participant. Energised by these living threads, the work appears to breathe alongside the surrounding room.

Contributing to themes of liveliness within these traditionally inert materials are Vicuña’s ideas surrounding the “not yet”. This open-ended phrase points toward notions of becoming and transformation.

Vicuña views existence as an ongoing process, rather than something fixed or finite. Swaying, mobile and fragile, her installations are literally untethered, resisting the urge to impose rigid meaning and leaving room for pure possibility. Through the “not yet” of Quipu Menstrual, Vicuña surrenders control, passing the work’s ongoing life over to the piece itself and the participating viewer.
Invisible threads of connection

Gallery three comprehensively introduces visitors to Vicuña’s vital role in Artist’s for Democracy (AFD). Vicuña was a founding member of this London-based artist group (alongside Guy Brett, John Dugger and David Medalla) which raised awareness within the arts and wider community of the plight of the Chilean people and other liberation and human rights struggles worldwide.
In existing literature, Vicuña has been cast in more of a supporting role in the formation of AFD, so it is refreshing that Whitechapel are championing her pivotal position as founding member.

There is photographic documentation of a smiling enthusiastic Vicuña in a 1974 exhibition showing her Objects for the Chilean Resistance, 1973-74. This series of objects highlights her focus on the overlooked and discarded within daily life revealing an intense desire for equality. The prolifically produced objects point towards an anxiety at being far from home during that politically unstable period of extreme and violent displays of power and forceful suppression.

The exhibition showcases the breadth of Vicuña’s multidisciplinary practice. It features a dedicated gallery for her surrealist-inflected paintings. These works are modern recreations of early canvasses lost or destroyed during her decades of exile and displacement between London, Colombia and New York.

The exhibition shows that Vicuña mourns the loss of these early paintings. But their rebirth here aligns beautifully with her belief in cyclic time and invisible threads of connections. There is a coherence here where dissolution becomes a creative catalyst rather than a destructive force.

Whitechapel completes the weaving in and out of our journey through Vicuña’s career by presenting the work Foraging Quipu (2025-26). This piece encapsulates Vicuña’s desire for communal engagement, transformation and viewer participation by requesting that the public contribute items that they have encountered within their daily routine.

Principally composed of natural and biological matter, Foraging Quipu is constantly decomposing and changing. Moving bodies around the work and the natural passage of time mean that Foraging Quipu will provide a different experience upon each look, illustrating some of Vicuña’s ideas about relationality and invisible living threads.
Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads is at Whitechapel Gallery, London, until February 14 2027.
