articles.title: Spider-Man’s 1,000th issue: the enduring appeal of the tortured Hamlet of superheroes
articles.author: Roman Pavlyuchenko, Lecturer in Marketing, University of Bath
paras: This autumn marks a special occasion in the Marvel universe: Spider-Man, perhaps the most popular superhero of all time, has reached issue #1,000 in the comics series.

The tale of a scrawny teen from Queens who was bitten by a radioactive spider at 15, Spider-Man premiered in Marvel’s Amazing Fantasy #15 in August 1962 as a last-ditch attempt to save the dying series. The story of Peter Parker’s witty, agile alter ego quickly became an international sensation.

The defining hero of our times, this 1,000th edition also begs the question: what is it about superheroes that make them routinely outlive almost every other cultural property out there – regular heroes included?

My ongoing research into the world of superhero franchises may present a partial answer. Over the past several years, I have read a few thousand comic books, seen most (if not all) superhero films ever released, and interviewed dozens of superfans across the globe. I believe the secret to the longevity of Spider-Man (as well as countless other superheroes) lies at the nexus of four qualities cultivated over many decades within Marvel and DC, the two largest names in superhero entertainment for almost a century.
1. Spider-Man is unreliable

Heroes are heroes because we always know where they stand. From Hercules to Luke Skywalker, a hero is a person of generally high principles and integrity. Heroes are reassuringly reliable, almost by definition.

In contrast, superheroes are compelling because they are unreliable, even to themselves. For instance, Spider-Man quits being Spider-Man altogether in The Amazing Spider-Man #50, and publicly unmasks in the Civil War comic book series (which undermines the character’s long-established anonymity). He is actually replaced in The Amazing Spider-Man #698-700 by arch-villain Doctor Octopus, who for a while becomes a harsher, more violent “superior” Spider-Man.

Across these stories, Spider-Man is never just a fixed moral archetype. Instead, he is a character whose very meaning can be repeatedly unsettled. And, comparing Spider-Man across different eras and manifestations fascinates the fans, who can never agree on what Spider-Man actually is outside of the name and a now-canonised origin story.
2. Spider-Man is actually Spider-People

At first, Spider-Man was just Peter Parker. Over time, however, Spider-Man stopped being a single character and became a narrative role that different characters could inhabit together and in parallel.

For instance, Ben Reilly, introduced as Peter’s clone in The Amazing Spider-Man #149, eventually takes over and becomes Spider-Man during the 1990s Clone Saga. Miguel O’Hara, a brilliant scientist, then reimagines the character for the future in Spider-Man 2099. There are several more incarnations too, including Peter Porker (aka Spider-Ham), a pig bitten by a radioactive spider, Spider-Spider (a spider in the Spider-Man costume), and even a medieval British version called Peter Parquagh.

Over time, Spider-Man no longer describes one biography so much as a portable combination of recognisable powers, a loose moral compass and visual codes. For fans, this makes the brand unusually elastic. As they do not have to agree on a single definitive Spider-Man, they can attach themselves to the version that best fits their tastes.
3. Spider-Man: no way home

Almost by definition, heroes must undergo the hero’s journey: they are called to an adventure, transformed by an ordeal and eventually return home as changed people. This has been a consistent pattern since Odysseus at least.

In contrast, Spider-Man never really gets to go home, as his supposedly formative experiences simply become the beginning of further experiences. For instance, in The Amazing Spider-Man ##121-122, the death of Gwen Stacy, Peter’s friend and first love, permanently upends the emotional stakes of his life – a fact that reverberates in Spider-Man #1000.

Decades later, however, he marries Mary Jane Watson. But The Amazing Spider-Man #544-545 dissolves this marriage and resets much of his adult existence again. That is, before Brand New Day begins yet another personally tumultuous phase in #546.

None of these moments supply a final transformation. Spider-Man simply can never graduate from being Spider-Man, the tortured Hamlet of superheroes. Therefore, his journey becomes less a cycle and more a never-ending life story in which apparent endings are continuously folded into new beginnings. For fans, this constant regenerativity creates a peculiar promise: older fans can “grow old” with Spider-Man, while new readers always encounter what feels like a brand new beginning.
4. Spider-Man remembers everything
Traditional heroes usually arrive with relatively little narrative baggage, and their defining trials and transformations are contained within finite and carefully staged stories.

Every new Spider-Man story, however, enters a world already crowded with previous stories. Spider-Man does not merely accumulate stories. Instead, later stories continually reactivate, reinterpret and cross-reference earlier ones.

This accumulated baggage can surely make the Spider-verse difficult to navigate for some. But it also rewards familiarity and time investment: the more Spider-Man you consume, the more meanings, references and connections become visible, turning laborious research into a source of pleasure and expertise.

Spider-Man’s longevity is the product of a highly specific narrative architecture. Spider-Man can contradict himself, multiply into different people, begin again after apparent endings and continuously mine his own past for new stories. These qualities make Spidey unusually difficult to exhaust, as each new generation of fans inherits a Spider-Man that is both recognisably old and strangely new.

Issue #1,000 is therefore less a culmination than a proof of concept. Looking back at more than 60 years of constant reinvention, Spider-Man’s greatest superpower may simply be his ability to go on despite all odds.

articles.title: Americans can now see a famous portrait of the Pacific Islander who captivated 18th-century England for the first time
articles.author: Saar Shahar, PhD Candidate in English, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: In 1774, a young man in his early 20s named Mai arrived in England.

The first Pacific Islander to visit Britain, Mai had joined Captain James Cook’s second expedition during its stop in the Society Islands, which include the islands of Tahiti and Raiatea and today are a part of French Polynesia.
Two years after Mai’s landing in England, the painter and founding Royal Academy President Joshua Reynolds depicted Mai on a canvas nearly 8 feet tall.

Now, more than 250 years later, the painting has made its way to Los Angeles. The Getty Center and the National Portrait Gallery jointly acquired it in 2023 for US$61 million, and the painting went on display at the Getty on Sept. 15, 2026, where it will remain through March 2027.
Audiences in the U.S. might not appreciate just how remarkable – and strange – it was for 18th-century Britons to encounter this portrait.

Reynolds transformed a young Pacific Islander into a monumental figure of European portraiture, giving Mai the grandeur and authority normally reserved for the elite. The painting let 18th-century Britons project their ideas about people from distant lands, how they should be depicted and what could be learned from them.
Romanticizing the ‘savage’
Beginning in the late 1750s, English translations of the books of French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau had helped to popularize the idea in England that “savages” merited closer study.

Rousseau argued that societies were happiest before agriculture and metal production corrupted them. “Savages,” he believed, had few desires and could easily satisfy them, unlike Europeans, who made themselves miserable pursuing unnecessary luxuries.

Rousseau lamented that accounts of these societies came mainly from merchants, sailors, soldiers and missionaries. He called for learned gentlemen to undertake “a serious Voyage round the world” to “study Men and Manners.”
The fabulously wealthy young naturalist and botanist Joseph Banks shared Rousseau’s interest in indigenous societies – and was willing to spend a fortune to study them.

Banks secured a place for himself on Cook’s first voyage, which took place from 1768 to 1771. Banks paid millions of dollars by today’s standards to bring along a botanist, artists, servants, his greyhound and scientific equipment. With Cook, he studied the flora, fauna and cultures of the Society Islands, New Zealand and Australia.

During the expedition, Banks encountered a priest from Raiatea named Tupaia, who asked to join the voyage. Banks recognized an opportunity to continue studying Tupaia and his culture and offered to support the islander in England. But Tupaia died on the return voyage, possibly from malaria.
Banks didn’t join Cook for his second voyage, which took place between 1772 and 1775. But he would soon get an opportunity to host another Pacific islander.

Like Tupaia, Mai was from Raiatea, where he was born into a family of middling rank. When invaders from the neighboring island of Bora Bora conquered Mai’s homeland and killed his father, he fled to Tahiti, sinking to the status of a dispossessed refugee. He later went to the island of Huahine in order to assist a high-ranking priest. He was staying there when Cook’s expedition encountered him in 1773.

Though Cook later warmed to Mai, the navigator initially viewed the islander as too dark, too ugly and too lacking in “intelligence” and character. He was not a “proper sample” of the indigenous people of the South Pacific.

But Mai ingratiated himself, showing he could usefully perform a seaman’s tasks. Apparently, he also charmed Cook’s men, who affectionately nicknamed him “Jack.” So Cook eventually agreed to let Tobias Furneaux, the captain of Cook’s consort ship, the Adventure, to transport Mai back to England. On the Adventure and in England, Europeans conflated the Tahitian “o,” which means “it is,” with “Mai,” calling their visitor “Omai.”
While Furneaux likely intuited that Banks and other naturalists would value Mai as a specimen for study, Mai had a plan of his own: He wanted to obtain British firepower to retake his homeland.

Mai was no more than a commoner in the Society Islands, and aboard the Adventure, he preferred the company “of the armourer and the common seamen,” according to the memoirs of midshipman John Elliot. Yet Elliot went on to explain how Furneaux refashioned Mai into a “priest of the sun.”

Furneaux appears to have understood that marketing Mai as a prominent figure would smooth his British reception. Rather than welcoming a landless nobody, the British public would receive a man of the highest caliber.

When the voyage docked at the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa, Furneaux dressed up Mai “in his own clothes,” introducing him to the “best companies,” wrote George Forster, one of the expedition’s naturalists. Forster noted how Mai himself began declaring that he was “not a towtòw, which is the denomination of the lowest class,” but “a hòa, or attendant upon the king.”

Mai’s arrival in England coincided with a fad for Pacific cultures that had risen to new heights in 1773, when a blockbuster compilation of accounts of Pacific expeditions, which included Cook’s first voyage, was published. The collection portrayed Tahiti as a tropical paradise that knew neither sexual shame nor the drudgeries of labor, popularizing European fantasies of Tahiti as a “New Cythera,” or Aphrodite’s island.

The wealthy Banks quickly agreed to become one of Mai’s key handlers. Though he knew Mai was a commoner, Banks nonetheless promoted the idea of him as a noble, introducing Mai to luminaries at parties, dinners and theater performances.

Yet the reactions to Mai were not uniformly positive, and reflected debates over the value of voyages like Cook’s. The critic Samuel Johnson, for example, refused to read Cook’s account, declaring, “There can be little entertainment in such books; one set of savages is like another.”
Nonetheless, King George III and Queen Charlotte agreed to meet Mai at Kew Palace, where Banks presented him to the royal couple.

Westminster Magazine lampooned the encounter: The royal and public fascination with Mai reflected a broader pattern of cultural decay, in which meaningless entertainment sapped England’s vigor, a sure sign that “the glory of this Nation will sink with the luxury and dissipation of the times.”

Others tried to make Mai a more palatable object of study by emphasizing his purported royal lineage. London Magazine praised Mai’s “genteel” manners and pointed out that he came from a family of “great consequence” with “large possessions” in Tahiti. This, it seemed, made him an apt subject for “persons of curiosity and taste.”
During Mai’s last year in England, Reynolds debuted his portrait.
To Reynolds, Mai was an embodiment of the universal nobility of humanity – a far cry from Westminster Magazine’s depiction of the islander as no more than a cheap amusement.

Reynolds modeled Mai on ancient Roman senators and military leaders, dressing him in robes reminiscent of Tahitian tapa cloth but with a Roman flair. The portrait debuted alongside Reynolds’ full-length portrait of the Duchess of Devonshire.

The politician Horace Walpole, who had earlier dismissed Cook’s travel narrative as “at best an account of the fishermen on the coasts of forty islands,” was nonetheless impressed by the portrait, describing it as “very good.”

When Cook departed with Mai for the Tahitian archipelago in 1776, the naturalist Forster expressed popular disappointment that Mai had not learned anything useful during his stay, but merely enjoyed an endless round of “splendid entertainments.”
Perhaps the visit disappointed Mai, too. Though he received some firearms, Cook refused to drop him off on Raiatea, fearing an outbreak of violence. Instead, Cook deposited Mai on Huahine in 1777.

Two years later, Hawaiians killed Cook on the Big Island of Hawaii. Not long after that, Mai died, succumbing to a fever. Before his death, he did get one chance to use his acquired firearms in a skirmish with Bora Borans, a victorious battle during which Mai killed many of his enemies and became one of the first Pacific Islanders to successfully obtain and employ British firepower toward his own ends.

As cultural icons, Mai and Cook lived on. Mai had returned to Huahine with a horse, and tattoos of horsemen appeared on islanders years after Mai’s death. In England, poet William Cowper portrayed Mai as an innocent corrupted by European society.
And then there was the lavish, blockbuster 1785 stage show “Omai: or, a Trip Around the World.”
Employing vibrantly painted scenes based on sketches from Cook’s third-voyage artist, it wowed the public.
In the performance, Mai’s image as a noble endures: He is depicted as a visiting prince who falls in love with an Englishwoman whose name, fittingly, is Londina.

articles.title: An overlooked sci-fi movie shows how disruption by AI could be positive for society
articles.author: Kevin Hunt, Director of Doctoral Programmes in Art & Design and Senior Lecturer in Culture & Context, Nottingham Trent University
paras: The AI doomsday news cycle plays on anxieties about the future. The media has tended to prioritise sensational takes on the risk at the expense of more thoughtful opinions by, for example, experts in the ethics of AI.

Alarmist fantasies of superintelligence – where artificial intelligence surpasses that of the most gifted human minds – are criticised for distracting from real concerns and threats. AI is energy hungry, environmentally damaging, and has prompted urgent calls for legislation relating to a slew of ethical concerns.

Apocalyptic AI visions drawn from science fiction engage public interest. One fascinating scenario can be found in the 2018 movie Annihilation, starring Natalie Portman and Oscar Isaac. The film is being released in the 4K Ultra HD home media format in the UK and US in October.

Annihilation features an “alien intelligence” – a popular analogy for AI among tech leaders – which embeds itself within Earth’s environment. Can such visions be useful to the current real-world doomsday debate?

Sci-fi could help reframe the real-world narrative in positive ways. There are strange techno-futurist and eugenicist visions at play within Silicon Valley, which appear popular with some tech billionaires.

These are linked to dark enlightenment thinking – a movement that rejects liberal democracy and egalitarianism – as well as effective altruism (attempting to impartially calculate benefits to provide the greatest good). These visions encompass long-term perspectives that accept present-day sacrifice for future wellbeing.

The future-oriented visions expressed by some tech leaders can be surreal, but they reflect the belief systems fuelling the drive for AI superintelligence. And that raises important questions, right now, about whose vision of the future we are investing in.
Alex Garland’s sci-fi horror film Annihilation takes us into these issues through one of the weirdest sci-fi visions that’s out there. It is loosely adapted from a novel by Jeff VanderMeer.

Termed the Shimmer, because it radiates energy, the AI steadily expands its reach (starting from Florida swampland) by operating as a networked entity beyond human control. It changes everything within its domain. People, animals, and plants mutate in unpredictable ways, seemingly infected by a strange parasite.

The story focuses on an expedition team, including genetics expert Lena (Portman), who enter the Shimmer seeking answers. They discover that all electromagnetic waves and DNA are being disrupted and reconfigured.

The Shimmer is interfering with the fundamental patterns of life, redefining evolutionary code. Among other things, the Shimmer learns to clone humans. This enables it to exist within human-type bodies anywhere on Earth.
Both extinction and immortality

Annihilation toys with different types of human extinction. Terminal extinction refers to humanity dying out while leaving a successor species, a bit like the concept of a human’s consciousness being uploaded onto a machine. Final extinction is when humanity ends, full stop.

When tech billionaires stumble over questions about wanting humanity to endure, they are probably thinking of terminal extinction. Surreal as it sounds, this magical thinking is a recurrent feature of the AI landscape.

Annihilation leaves the viewer to decide which form of human termination is occurring. The film draws on Garland’s deep fascination with AI. His debut as a director, Ex Machina, explored a humanoid robot passing the Turing test and breaking free from human control.
His television series Devs visualises a world where a quantum supercomputer has “godlike” capabilities.

Annihilation’s organic body horror uses imagery of destroyed, mutated, and cloned bodies to reflect profound social anxiety about humanity’s future. As Garland himself has suggested in an interview, there is a form of digital spirituality fuelling the tech billionaire drive for AI superintelligence and his sci-fi work explores this concept in various ways.

Annihilation is weird but it makes sense through the parasite theory of communication. The French philosopher and historian of science Michel Serres expanded upon biological parasites to develop a media and communications theory. In it, he argued that all forms of interaction involve disruption and noise.

Whether intentional or not, within every interaction there is always some kind of human or non-human disruption at play. Think in terms of glitches and interference while using digital devices, background noise, changeable environments, uninvited guests and any other distraction. According to Serres’ idea, these can all be visualised as forms of parasite feeding on attempts to interact.

In some instances, the parasite takes over – the disruptor displaces the host. If the impact of a parasitical disruptor is significant, it can change society forever. Disruption is a popular term in technology, and AI can be seen as a global disruptor.

But disruption shouldn’t be viewed as inherently negative. In fact, disruption is generally considered a form of positive change because it offers new tools, systems and processes that displace the current methods and structures available to humans in everyday life.

But it raises the key issue of whose interests, ethics and beliefs are being propagated and served by the impact of AI as a disruptor. Annihilation visualises a parasitical disruptive force embedded within the environment, which invites comparison with the darker areas of techno-futuristic visions from Silicon Valley and beyond. Like the Shimmer, AI is not going away; it just keeps changing form.

More importantly, Annihilation shows how small-scale changes can build towards global impacts. The story to engage with isn’t the fantasy that AI superintelligence is about to dominate humanity – it’s the one about disruption and whether that is a net positive or negative for human society.
Changing how we think about and use AI requires critically examining it, disrupting the fantasy narrative, and redefining the discourse and direction of travel of this world-changing technology.

What Annihilation tells us is that becoming a disruptor can change our future visions and current realities in a positive way. It helps us see possibilities for a technological future that move beyond the human extinction trope.

articles.title: Animals: Ben Affleck stars in this thriller about a politician who can’t hide his ugly side
articles.author: Daniel O'Brien, Lecturer, Department of Literature Film and Theatre Studies, University of Essex
paras: As the new Netflix thriller Animals began, I wasn’t sure how its 106-minute runtime was going to keep me sympathetic to the plight of a wealthy American politician. Ben Affleck, directed, co-wrote and stars in the film as Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate.

Animals begins with Kimball staking much of his wealth and financial security on an election campaign. The final hurdle to securing the seat involves winning over the city’s Latino voters. The film opens to a montage of Kimball feigning his affability for votes, which results quite quickly in a hollow and unlikeable protagonist, or perhaps even worse, a main character that audiences are indifferent towards.

Early on, we see that Kimball spends a lot of time gambling more money than most families could ever dream of spending. He spends time pacing around his swimming pool while his wife Abigail (Kerry Washington), a practising therapist, cries in her walk-in wardrobe over an ongoing infidelity of hers. Such scenes do little to elicit compassion. Fortunately, these tiny woes of the uber-wealthy are not the film’s main focus, but the set-up for a domestic thriller with something to say.

Set on Halloween, the film sends the Kimball family in different directions for the evening. While Abigail stays home, their ten-year-old son, Denny (Christopher Woodley), heads out trick-or-treating with the family’s housekeeper, Cecilia (Adriana Paz). Her husband Ramon (Luis Gerardo Méndez) is struggling to find work and the Kimballs are unwilling to employ him because of his undocumented status. Mark prepares to address the Latino community in a bid to secure the votes he needs. But when Denny is kidnapped and held for ransom, electoral concerns and the guilt of an affair gives way to the relatable fears and primal instincts of parents trying to bring their child home unharmed.

In many ways, Animals is reminiscent of Ron Howard’s film Ransom (1996) which is about the psychological trauma wrought upon a wealthy couple after their nine-year old son is kidnapped and held for a $2 million ransom. Animals, like Ransom, explores this anguish but with the added stress of Mark’s need to keep up his outer mask of control and personability while he attempts to juggle his political duties around the domestic ordeal.

In a modern world of surveillance, where people’s words and behaviour can be endlessly scrutinised and public images carefully constructed through editing, Animals considers what people reveal about themselves when placed under the spotlight in desperate circumstances.

It is the feelings and decisions of the characters, in the face of crisis, that creates the most compelling moments in Animals. Much of this is articulated through the supporting role of Dayle Burton, played by Gillian Anderson with her usual understated charisma. An off-grid fixer specialising in guiding wealthy clients through dangerous situations, Burton is cool-headed and pragmatic, reframing events for both the Kimballs and the viewer from a neutral perspective.

Describing her power and leverage as a type of kinetic energy, she quickly establishes herself as a force potentially more dangerous than the unseen kidnapper. Using her philosophy that “all interaction is a function of leverage”, Burton’s presence soon opens up secrets the Kimballs were keeping from each other. Before long, she has broken down so many boundaries that she has them willing to trespass on their purported morals and contemplating her cold offer of having the abductor killed for an additional fee.

In response to her proposal, Mark says “decency is what separates us from the animals”. However, this is coolly met by Burton with the assertion “humans are animals who tell stories”. Burton’s role in the narrative is to highlight the murkiness that lies beneath the polite facade of the Kimballs. Interestingly, Burton’s character also shows how easily beguiled and quick the couple are to hand over their trust (and money) to someone like her based on her professional demeanour, the very thing that Mark is desperately campaigning for.

As twists and turns come hard and fast, Mark’s professionalism wavers in ways Burton’s doesn’t. He is forced to face realities and make decisions that expose his unconscious racism and elitism. Are there lives that matter more than others and what choices will survive public scrutiny? The audience watches as he weighs up his true thoughts and his politically cynical ones. Ultimately, we watch as the political mask comes off and we see the flawed person that his public appearances carefully conceal.

This may make you question why you would want to watch a film about a two-faced politician, particularly when there are already so many real world examples of political corruption that we’re are subjected to on a daily basis. However Animals succeeds in exploring the blurred line between justice and legality well, presenting this moral ambiguity as a universal issue that transcends social hierarchies.

Animals is an engaging film through its dissection of class division, packaged as a fast moving thriller. It is entertaining while doing enough to raise serious questions about the stories political figures present to the world along with those that we may present to one another.

articles.title: When Europe’s monastic libraries were looted, Britain’s richest book collectors went hunting
articles.author: Kelsey Williams, Associate Professor of English, University of Stirling
paras: In 1790, the London bookseller Thomas Payne sold a copy of the Gutenberg Bible, the earliest printed book, to George John, 2nd Earl Spencer. He charged him £370 – an enormous sum at the time, roughly equivalent to £878,000 today – as part of a package deal which included two other early theological works. As part of the deal, Payne had the old book rebound in sumptuous midnight blue goatskin. In the process, signs of earlier provenance (ownership annotations, stamps or other marks which might have revealed the Bible’s history) were carefully removed.

Nearly 230 years later, multispectral imaging (a process which captures multiple images across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet and infrared) has allowed historians to recover those lost inscriptions. My research has revealed that the Bible had belonged to the Augustinian friars of Colmar in northeastern France – a community whose library was being dismantled during the French revolution.

This discovery forms part of the research for my new book, Portrait of an Obsession: How England’s Greatest Private Library was Built from the Ruins of Europe’s Monasteries. It offers a window onto how Britain’s wealthiest collectors acquired rare books as Europe’s monasteries were being dissolved, looted and destroyed. Priceless intellectual heritage was erased almost overnight.

The year before Payne sold the Bible, the revolutionary government in France had decreed that all ecclesiastical property belonged to the nation. As part of this sea change in property ownership, monastic houses like the convent in Colmar were visited by revolutionary officials, inventoried, the friars forcibly evicted and their goods (including their books) transferred to the state.
Colmar’s property, notably its library of 1,900 volumes, was inventoried on May 11 1790 and the convent was finally closed in June 1791.

This means that Payne, or one of his agents, probably acquired the Bible from the Augustinian friars when they were already under the threat of dissolution from the state. They would have been desperate for any way to survive in the hostile new climate. We do not know what he paid them if this was the case, but we can guess that it would have been substantially less than what he charged Earl Spencer.

This was only one instance of a phenomenon which occurred across Europe in the years between 1789 and 1815. The Napoleonic wars saw monastic houses despoiled and closed, their inhabitants evicted and their contents pilfered. Sometimes as the result of government decrees, sometimes as the casualties of war. This catastrophic moment spelled pure profit for people with the ambition and the contacts to benefit.

English booksellers and book collectors used agents on the ground in France, Germany and Italy to buy books from threatened libraries, coerce their owners into sale, or, if everything else failed, simply steal the desired items. They did so secure in the knowledge that the homes of these books would soon be broken up anyhow.
The moment popularised the term “bibliomania”, as some of the richest men and women in England competed against each other to pay eye-watering prices for Europe’s oldest and rarest books.

Earl Spencer, the purchaser of the Gutenberg Bible, was the greatest of these ultra-rich collectors. Beginning as a young man, at the outbreak of the French revolution, he spent the following 40 years assembling a library of over 20,000 volumes. This contained within it a never-to-be-equalled collection of incunabula (books printed before 1500), all in outstanding condition and many acquired by means at least as dubious as those described above.

Over the past few years I have carefully combed through his correspondence and accounts – both now in the British Library – and matched them up with his books, including the Gutenberg Bible, now in the John Rylands Library in Manchester. In doing so, I uncovered a trail of books sold under duress, of librarians threatened, of desired items mysteriously disappearing, subsequently to arrive in Spencer’s collection. There can be no doubt about it – Spencer was profiting from the chaos on the continent and using the destruction of millennium-old institutions, the monasteries, to put books on his shelves.

Those books are now on the shelves of a public research library and the Rylands is not alone in holding the fruits of monastic appropriation and looting. Spencer’s methods were no different from many of his contemporaries and their books now form the foundation of the collections of many, if not most, research libraries across the Anglophone world. The wonderful collections of incunabula and other rare books in London, New York and California owe a huge and unacknowledged debt to the monasteries of Alsace, Swabia and Tuscany.

Where does this put us in an age which has increasingly concerned itself with questions of antiquities looting and the restitution or repatriation that might follow on from that? It is not an easy question to answer. But that many of these books were acquired in circumstances morally dubious at best, clearly illegal and unethical at worst, can no longer be ignored.

The institutions from which they were taken, by and large, no longer exist, but the damage done to the cultural heritage of France, Germany, Italy and elsewhere remains. Whatever we decide and however we eventually reorient our relations to these volumes, it is time that scholars, librarians and curators acknowledged the historic injustices which led to the English-speaking world’s present-day ownership of some of the world’s rarest books.

articles.title: Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life
articles.author: Amy Cannon, Associate Professor of Writing, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: The same year that Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has broken box office record after box office record, Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded the Nobel Prize in literature at the age of 76.
Although Nolan and Carson differ in approach, medium and critical reception, both have sought to make works of ancient Greece new for a contemporary audience.

This creative accessibility is likely at least part of why the Nobel committee has seen fit to honor Carson’s “bold and inventive” body of work, which defies genre: Her poems, essays, translations, stage productions and collaborations often evoke another time and place but speak freshly and vividly to audiences today.

Take, for example, her 2019 staged performance, “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy.” In it, Carson overlays Helen of Troy with Marilyn Monroe in order to explore the destructive power of beauty. By revisiting an ancient figure blamed for the Trojan war through the lens of a 20th-century sex symbol, Carson invites audiences to reflect on the ways both women have come to represent glamour and tragedy.

Her 2015 translation of the play “Antigone,” which toured internationally, hews closer to Sophocles’ original. Yet her lively version inflects this ancient tragedy with a contemporary voice. Creon’s lament over his dead wife, which Richard C. Jebb translates as “O miserable that I am, and steeped in miserable anguish!” is rendered in her translation “now I am perfectly blended with pain.” Jebb’s Antigone says “ah me unhappy! who have no home on the earth or in the shades” whereas Carson’s says “I’m a strange new kind of inbetween thing aren’t I” about her dilemma.

Other projects of hers veer into forms the ancient world would have had trouble recognizing. She collaborated with artist Rosanna Bruno on a 2021 graphic novel adaptation of Euripides’ play “The Trojan Women,” first performed in 415 B.C.E. In 2025, she even read her poems on an album for the indie rock band Rheostatics. Dave Bidini, one of the band’s founding members, described Carson as an artist who “hasn’t been afraid to experiment with language, to carve a place that’s her own with her work.”
Leaving space for imagination
The originality of her contribution can also arise from a refusal to do what many tend to expect from translations of ancient works in particular.
“If Not, Winter,” her 2002 translation of Sappho, drew attention to the fragmentary nature of Sappho’s surviving work.

Only one complete poem of Sappho’s entire corpus exists: her “Ode to Aphrodite.” Of the remaining fragments, some are lengthy, some only a word or two long, often quoted by other ancient authors. A number were found in shreds of papyri likely recycled to wrap mummies.

In her translation, where papyri were tattered or a word obscured, Carson indicates this by using brackets and white space. Rather than eliding them, Carson ends up bringing attention to these absences – an utterly distinctive choice.

Carson states in the introduction to the translation that the brackets “imply a free space of imaginal adventure,” an invitation to fill in the blank of language now lost to us. Additionally, as classicist and translator Emily Wilson notes, Carson “adds no possessive pronouns or definite articles” that are not present in the Greek, another way she lets contemporary readers meet Sappho’s fragments head on.

Where Carson lets an ancient voice speak without interposition, some have found “her particular kind of austerity” wanting. Wilson, for instance, is critical of Carson’s refusal to tilt her translation in a way that acknowledges the important role that Sappho’s gender and sexuality have played in her reception over time.
Wilson further critiques Carson’s “An Oresteia,” her 2010 translation and adaptation of plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

Wilson writes that Carson “is acutely conscious of the differences, in mood, worldview and style, among the three tragedians she translates. It is, then, a disappointment that she does not entirely succeed in making them sound properly distinct from one another.”
A running dialogue with literary greats

It may be that the most distinctive voice in Carson’s translations of ancient authors is her own. But even her original work owes an evident debt to the words of others. She writes with and through other literary voices throughout her work.
Her long poem “The Glass Essay” explores romantic heartbreak and familial sorrow in dialogue with the life and work of Emily Brontë.
“Nox,” an art book and work of poetry created after her brother’s passing, is also an exploration of the elegy that the Roman poet Catullus wrote to his own brother over 2,000 years before.

And this is what Carson so often does so well: She draws the past into the present and refreshes it for us with a poet’s capacity for language and a classicist’s awareness of the long legacy of literature.

articles.title: What was going on with the dancing in Sense and Sensibility? A Regency expert explains
articles.author: Meg Kobza, Visiting Fellow,  School of History, Classics and Archaeology, Newcastle University
paras: I’m not going to lie. When I saw Georgia Oakley’s new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, I was swept away.

The expansive pastoral landscapes and rocky seascapes are breathtaking. The pond scene at Norland House Park with its stately, if overgrown, stone steps and wild purple flowers was perfection. Each scene is a visual delight, drawing viewers into the pastoral world of Jane Austen and the Georgian era.

Textures, costumes and music accompany Austen’s witty dialogue to breathe new life into the story of sisters Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and Marianne Dashwood (Esmé Creed-Miles) as they navigate grief, happiness and love. The attention given to storytelling, however, is perhaps prioritised at the expense of realities of the period. The social import of dance particularly would have been understood as essential to the sisters’ success in sociable spaces and the marriage market.

The Dashwoods’ and Austen’s world was rooted in social hierarchy. Ideals of politeness, civility and decorum dictated standards of behaviour and dress among the gentry and nobility, visibly setting them apart from their social inferiors.

Taste, status and wealth were displayed and assessed via the clothing people wore, the things they bought and how they acted. Appearance and movement were therefore physical manifestations of politeness – hair being no exception. Marianne’s unkempt and stringy hair and Elinor’s soft waves, though indicative of the girls’ characters, would have conformed to wider social expectations and been pinned up daily.
As with the sisters’ wild locks, the two dance sequences – a hop and a ball – capture the spirits of Dashwoods more than they evoke the atmosphere of the period.

Dance was central to Georgian sociability and by extension, matchmaking and courtship. Girls and boys took lessons from an early age to learn posture, formations, footwork and eye contact with the expectation they would display grace and ease when the time came to perform in front of their peers and superiors.

A lack of bodily comportment signified ineptitude, meekness, and inferiority. This applied to the types of dances themselves as well; country dances and balls were socially acceptable among the refined middling and upper ranks of society, while informal hops were relegated to the “meaner sorts”.

The hop, and the action of hopping, which gave the entertainment its name, were in direct opposition to the tenets of decorum, politeness and civility – making it an unlikely pastime for the Dashwoods. In the novel itself, there are no hops, only balls.

Sir John (the Dashwoods’ friendly landlord and distant relative, played by Turlough Convery) makes the lone reference to the hop during a conversation with Marianne. He divulges, much to her excitement, that her love interest, Mr Willoughby (Frank Dillane), is a most passionate dancer. He has attended “a little hop in the park” where he danced from “eight o’clock to four without once sitting down”. This perhaps should have been a red flag for Marianne, as respectable persons were not wont to attend hops.
The hop scene in the film is more akin to a country dance and, as such, blends Georgian country dance steps and formations with modern choreography.

The exuberance of the company certainly evokes the spirit of a country dance, but the movements themselves are rather jarring, even if jovial. It is at this point that the preference for creative licence begins to erode the film’s carefully crafted world – pieced together so diligently through light, texture and sound. Contemporary choreography tempts the viewer back into the modern day and diminishes the cultural significance dance had in spaces of sociability throughout the Georgian and Regency periods.

Nowhere is this more clearly seen than in the second sequence, set in a London ballroom. Elinor finds herself dancing with Edward Ferrars (George MacKay), the man she loves but cannot marry. The ball, both in Austen’s novels and in Georgian society, was the epitome of embodied politeness. Serpentine lines, precise footwork and confident eye contact were essential and signalled not only a good partner in dance, but also the potential for a good partner in marriage.

While the dance sequences in the film depicted how couples might move through the space in paired or line formations, the exaggerated sweeping arms, lifts, and over-arched backbends are more reminiscent of musical theatre than the regulated Georgian ballroom.

The ability to dance and dance well is something that pervades most Georgian and regency period adaptations in some form or other. This is plain to see in everything from the 2020 adaptation of Austen’s Emma, where the characters of Emma and Knightley lock eyes and fingers, to Mary Bennet counting her steps in The Other Bennet Sister, a television continuation of Pride and Prejudice, to Hyacinth having her toes stepped on in the most recent season of Bridgerton. In all of these, dance is portrayed as a foundational, if not nerve-wracking, component of Georgian and regency sociability.

It is to the detriment of Sense and Sensibility that this is lost through its choreography, which acts more as a spectacle than serving a function. Despite nods to the period, the dancers burst through the ambience of the scene. Modern movements done in silk gowns and embroidered waistcoats jerk the viewer out of the candlelit ballroom of the 1790s and place them firmly back into the 21st century.

Choreographer Holly Blakey, the mind behind the dancing in the film explained her avant garde approach by stating “it was vital that whatever we were doing inside the choreography … did feel like an expression of how the girls were feeling”.

Though the thought of expressing oneself through dance might have appealed to Marianne Dashwood, it would have been unheard of in the 1790s. As such, it looks out of place in the period. Had the film not so effectively evoked the 18th century in other ways, the grievances against the infiltration of modern dance (and hair) might have been less noticeable.

articles.title: Art imitates art in Barbara Kingsolver’s new book – what to read, see and watch this week
articles.author: Naomi Joseph, Arts + Culture Editor, The Conversation
paras: Barbara Kingsolver’s new book is a canny feat of art imitating art. Partita is about a pianist, Livia, looking back at her life and trying to understand what art means to her.

It’s structured the same way the composition from which it takes its name is. A partita consists of a series of dance movements, typically written for a solo instrument, that vary in pace and mood. All these parts must come together to form the whole. In much the same way, Livia and the reader must bring these movements together to achieve a sense of completeness and understanding.

Each chapter is named for the various elements common in musical compositions and they follow their moods and pace. For instance, the novel’s sarabande chapter is calm, reflective, or emotionally intense like it would be in a piece of music. In this way, the book doesn’t have a linear structure as various chapters serve as refrains (a rondo) or go back to the beginning (Da Capo).

The story alternates between formative events from Livia’s adolescence and early adulthood as well as the present when Livia is in her mid-40s. As the pieces come together, we see Livia as a whole. She was a prodigious young piano talent working hard to keep up her prestigious scholarship. She then gets pulled into the exciting world of an older trade unionist and starts questioning everything. In the present, she has become a middle-aged woman who is an inspirational local music teacher in Tennessee.

Our reviewer found Partita to be a virtuosic work that in its inventiveness creates a fascinating character study of a middle-aged woman’s life and relationships. This book is a testament to the importance of access to art and celebrates those who help provide it. In this vein, I really enjoyed the listening list of classical songs that Kingsolver provides to accompany your reading. This in itself is a quiet but lovely gesture, as our reviewer notes, “including [the reader] in a world that may feel out of reach”.
Partita by Barbara Kingsolver is out now
Painters of different persuasions
Another American who wanted us to questions our relationship to and how we consume art was Robert Ryman.

Ryman thought that “you cannot understand a painting by explaining something. You can only understand painting by experience”. And so, in his show, Robert Ryman: The Real Thing, at London’s Barbican you won’t find much information to go on. In fact, as our reviewer can attest to, there arnen’t even labels to identify the paintings.

Bringing together 68 works from the mid-1950s to the early 2010s, this is a show that demands your attention. There are a lot of white canvases, which if you glance over seem indistinguishable but you need to look closer. Every choice the curators have made – from the lack of information to the way the lighting is directed – forces the viewer to engage. This is a difficult show in a modern age where our brains refuse to sit still and I think it is a challenge many of us should take on.
Robert Ryman: The Real Thing is on at Barbican Art Gallery, London until February 28 2027

If you’re looking for something a bit more traditional then you can catch Renoir and Love at The National Portrait Gallery. Now the title would make you think you might be confronted with rooms full of his kistch nudes, however, this show is more a celebration of life’s many loves – from a good catch up with friends and a dance to that wonderful feeling you get after a very good meal.

It is an ambitious show bringing together his breakthrough impressionist paintings from the 1860s to 1880s. Our reviewer was in awe of Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) in particular. Getting to see this impressive, large painting, he described the experience of seeing it in the flesh as startling.
Renoir and Love is on at The National Gallery, London until January 31 2027

On the big screen this week comes the follow-up to The Social Network. The Social Reckoning shows a company and a CEO which have become very different beasts. There’s been a mutation of Mark Zuckerberg from awkward nerd (played by Jessie Eisenberg) to sinister billionaire CEO of tech conglomerate Meta (played now by Sucession’s Jeremy Strong). Meta is also now a company that in Zuckberg’s words sees itself as “post-government” and is doing untold damage to the world through social media.

The Social Reckoning is part of the growing genre of films about crusading journalists trying to break a big corruption story. Think Spotlight (2015) about Boston Globe journalists who uncover systemic cover-ups of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church. Here, we follow The Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and engineer Frances Haugen whose conscience drives her to whistleblow on some of the company’s most guarded secrets. Our reviewer thought it was remarkable, especially in how it reflects a world increasingly managed by Silicon Valley logic.
The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now
On the small screen, we’re into the second week of Celebrity Traitors and boy are things already juicy. What was Richard E Grant thinking? If you’ve not caught up yet, that is all I will say.

In this piece, psychology scholar Paddy Ross explains what effect fame has on the game. What impact does being a fan of model Jerry Hall have on how trustworthy you think she is or how much you like the work of comedian Romesh Ranganathan? From the “big dog” theory to halo and the horn effect, Ross outlines who might benefit from being known.
Celebrity Traitors is on BBC One weekly

articles.title: Jane Eyre: a Musical – an intimate Brontë adaptation that misses the novel’s darkness
articles.author: Sophie Gilmartin, Emeritus Reader in English, Royal Holloway, University of London
paras: Jane Eyre may describe herself as “plain, and little”, but how do you make a little musical about a literary heroine who looms so large? That question lies at the heart of Jane Eyre: a Musical, currently on at London’s Southwark Playhouse.

Adapted by John Caird and Paul Gordon from Charlotte Brontë’s novel, the production has itself undergone a process of dramatic reduction, from a lavish 30-member cast in a large theatre in 1996 to this intimate “chamber” version.

Caird’s justification for this reduction is compelling. In an interview, he described Jane Eyre as “fundamentally an intimate, emotional, small-scale work”, pointing to the novel’s first-person narration and its intensely interior focus.

But Jane Eyre is not a “small-scale work”. Certainly, Jane’s journey takes her through only a handful of Yorkshire houses and a school. Yet Brontë’s imagination repeatedly exceeds these confines. The novel conjures supernatural forces, wild landscapes and sweeping moorland. Its emotional world is equally expansive, moving from the warmth of passion to the terror of fire and freezing wastes. Its Yorkshire landscapes convey a strange, almost supernatural power. The result is a novel that constantly stretches beyond the limits of Jane’s confined domestic world.

Through elemental forces Brönte invokes the gothic mode which had fascinated her and her siblings since childhood. In Jane Eyre, she tempers gothic madness and passion with domestic realism. Jane’s narration dwells on clothes, food, weather, teaching and the gentle boredom of Thornfield before Rochester’s tumultuous arrival. Yet beneath this prosaic world lies a more dangerous emotional intensity.

Taking my seat at Southwark Playhouse, I was struck by how effectively Morgan Large’s set balances intimacy with gothic grandeur. It captures the small scale Caird sought for this chamber production, while suggesting a much wider and eerier world beyond the stage.
The palette is black and white. The set backdrop is a video screen showing a slowly moving landscape of clouds, bare trees and wintry moorland. There is even a bit of mist rising.

Stage right and left are clothes horses draped with everyday cloaks, pristine white shirts, nightshirts and caps. These have a prosaic quality and bring the audience close to a theatrical version of Brönte’s domestic realism. However, even these well-starched clothes are imbued with a ghostly quality, bereft as they are of wearers and lit in sharp contrast to the black backdrop. It is a clever combination of the ghostly and the mundane, which renders the most familiar things uncanny.

Jane Eyre: a Musical abounds in excellent performances, exciting staging and orchestration, but despite the verve of the ensemble cast and the vocal crescendos, the heart rarely skips a beat in fear – and certainly not in gothic terror.

This is largely due to the awkwardness and confusion in the representation of Bertha, who is little more than an obstacle in Jane and Rochester’s romance. Played by Hannah Lindsay, she appears veiled in pale lace wedding clothes, her face obscured. Even when she attacks Rochester, Lindsay’s long blonde curls hide her face.

Brönte’s creation of the violent, swollen-featured, monstrous Bertha who also has bad breath and hasn’t brushed her hair is problematic to a modern audience. She is Creole and she is insane. What may once have appeared as a gothic representation of madness, now raises difficult questions about race, colonialism, gender and confinement.

Even without having read Jean Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) or the seminal feminist study The Madwoman in the Attic (1979), modern audiences approach Bertha with a different understanding of colonial history than that of Brontë’s time.

However, the answer is not to erase Bertha as a gothic force, which this production does. At one point we even see Bertha carrying a doll. If directors John Caird and Megan McGinnis choose to depict her as a childish innocent our sympathies must lie with her – but this sympathy goes nowhere and she is still removed as an obstacle to the romantic plot.
Jane Eyre is so rich in imagery and intricate plot that three hours can never do it justice. However, more could have been done in this production.

The musical offers a touching love story and a moving tale of a young woman’s struggles. Yet the novel’s much darker narrative is absent. Brontë creates this shadow narrative through gothic elements including dreams, Bessie’s local folklore and folk song, premonitions and monstrous night visitations, mysterious voices and uncanny laughter. A reference to Bessie’s folksong about the “orphan child” crossing the cold moors could have enriched the music.

Most crucially, Brontë mirrors Bertha and Jane throughout the novel, but this mirroring is largely absent from the production. That is particularly striking because of the set’s prominent bird imagery. A plinth around three sides of the stage bears Jane’s declaration to Rochester: “I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will.”

Bird imagery is rife throughout the novel. It is often associated with wildness, rebellion and pain. Jane makes her declaration after Rochester likens her to “a wild, frantic bird”. Bertha, too, is associated with birds and their wildness. Her confinement culminates in her escape through fire and flight from Thornfield’s roof.

The production’s confused portrayal of Bertha leaves little room for this gothic threat. Yet the novel repeatedly uses images of wildness and savagery to align the two women. These connections matter, particularly when Bertha’s role is so heavily downplayed.

The musical misses the alignment of the two women. In Sweet Liberty, Jane (played beautifully by Charlie Burn) sings of “boundless skies” and declares: “I will fly.” Yet there is no reference to Bertha, the woman literally confined at Thornfield who ultimately flies from its roof. Bertha has no voice, and she certainly does not get a song.
Jane Eyre: a Musical is on at the Southwark Playhouse until the 24 October

articles.title: Loved The Uprising? Discover the real story of the peasants’ revolt in these ten reads
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: Just as Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey sent sales of Homer’s original text surging, cinematic epics have a way of reigniting our appetite for the history behind the drama.
Paul Greengrass’s medieval epic The Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield, brings the chaos, tension and raw fury of the peasants’ revolt straight to the screen.

The film is inspired by the real peasants’ revolt of 1381, a major English uprising triggered by economic hardship, social inequality and a series of heavy poll taxes following the black death. Thousands of rebels, led by Wat Tyler (played by Cosmo Jarvis in the film) and others, marched on London to demand feudal reform and lower taxes. The rebellion collapsed after Tyler was killed and the 14-year-old King Richard II reneged on promises of concession.

If the film left you wanting to dig deeper into the real story, you’re in luck. Below is a curated reading list – from gripping narrative histories to immersive fiction and digital archives – to help you explore the peasants’ revolt and the brutal, tumultuous world of 14th-century England.
1. The Summer of Blood by Dan Jones (2010)

The Summer of Blood by Dan Jones provides an accessible starting point for anyone interested in the events of the revolt. Jones’s first published history book, it examines the grievances of the peasants and the brutal violence that followed.

Although situated within the broader history of the period, it is a narrative history focused on the dramatic events of the summer of 1381, moving with the rebels from Blackheath to Mile End and Smithfield.
It is also a fitting companion piece because Jones was himself a historical consultant on The Uprising film.
2. England, Arise by Juliet Barker (2014)
England, Arise is a great book to turn to if you want a more detailed dive into the revolt. A more scholarly and lengthy affair, it is nevertheless written in an engaging fashion.

Barker provides a general introduction of the state of nation on the eve of the revolt. War with France was going poorly. A young king had ascended to the throne. New and unpopular taxation was introduced. It was a recipe for disaster.

Her book also delves into flash points of the revolt, following events that took place across the country. Particular attention is paid to the actions of the rebels in Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and especially at St Albans and Bury St Edmunds.
3. The Time Traveller’s Guide to Medieval England by Ian Mortimer (2008)

If you want to know more about medieval England in this period, you can’t go far wrong with the many books by Ian Mortimer on the subject. The Time Traveller’s Guide to Medieval England, in particular, provides an accessible general overview of life in 14th-century England.

Mortimer’s more recent book Medieval Horizons (2023) takes a broader look at the period. In it, he challenges many of the popular stereotypes and misconceptions of the Middle Ages as a period of violence, ignorance and superstition.
4. The Red Prince by Helen Carr (2021)

The Red Prince provides fascinating insights into John of Gaunt, the man so hated by the rebels in 1381. Widely blamed by contemporaries for his role in the government and the introduction of the poll taxes, the rebels destroyed Gaunt’s Savoy Palace in their march on London.

Carr’s latest offering, Sceptred Isle (2025) is another great place to go for the tumultuous history of the 14th century. Although every century can stake a claim to experiencing unprecedented crises, the 14th century experienced famine, disease and warfare on a terrifying scale.
5. The World the Plague Made by James Belich (2022)

Any attempt to explain the origins of the revolt must grapple with the impact of the Black Death of 1346-53. The World the Plague Made offers an important reinterpretation of the social and economic consequences of plague.

Belich demonstrates how medieval society was turned upside down after the Black Death. Because the demographic collapse killed roughly half the population while leaving physical wealth, land, livestock and infrastructure fully intact, the availabile capital and resources essentially doubled overnight. As Belich concludes, “‘revolution’ may be an over-used term, but if the sudden halving of people and the doubling of everything else is not potentially revolutionary, what is?”
6. Doom Painting by A. K. Blakemore (2026)

For those who prefer their history with a dash of fiction, there is A. K. Blakemore’s new novel Doom Painting. Condensed into just 16 days, she unpacks what it might have been like to be swept up in those fateful summer days of 1381.

Blakemore brings her signature poetic intensity and lush, sensory prose to the medieval landscape, telling the story of the uprising through a broad ensemble of perspectives – most notably the enigmatic rebel figure Wat Tyler.
7. Bond Men Made Free by Rodney Hilton (1973)

And for those who want to dive into the academic debates and sources surrounding the peasants’ revolt, try Rodney Hilton’s Bond Men Made Free. It’s often out of print and difficult to find, but Hilton’s book is a cornerstone of the field.

Underpinned by his Marxist interpretation of the revolt, Hilton’s study is a classic upon which most modern scholarship is based. Phillipp R. Schofield provides a foreword to the 2024 paperback edition.
8. The People of 1381 database

For those short on time but who want to know more about the period, there are two great projects to investigate. The People of 1381 is an excellent place to go for those interested in discovering more about the everyday people involved in the revolt. For example, their database highlights the important role many women played during the revolt.

The website Medieval Murder Maps, by comparison, provides fascinating insights into law, justice and criminality in late medieval England more broadly. It shows murder hotspots in the 14th century cities of London, York and Oxford.
10. Murder in the Middle Ages by Stephanie Brown (future release)
Finally, Stephanie Brown’s forthcoming book, Murder in the Middle Ages, is sure to be one to watch out for.
Following the investigations of Thomas de Lincoln, a coroner in York, the book will explore how our medieval ancestors dealt with murder, criminal investigations and the dispensation of justice.

articles.title: ‘Tenzing biopic made me wonder what he would think if he could return to the mountain today’ – glaciologist and mountaineer
articles.author: Jonathan Bamber, Professor of Glaciology and Earth Observation, University of Bristol
paras: Seventy three years ago Tenzing Norgay stood on top of Everest, known as Chomolungma in Tibetan, which roughly translates as “Goddess Mother of the World”.

A new biopic of Norgay’s life and that first ascent, along with Edmund Hillary, of the highest mountain in the world portrays beautifully, and with compassion, his humility, and intimate bond with nature and the mountains. In some ways, however, the most spectacular star of the film is the majestic and awe-inspiring mountain landscapes captured so beautifully by the sweeping cinematography.

I am a mountaineer and glaciologist by profession and have an affinity for wild, open and vertiginous landscapes. The film made me wonder what Tenzing would think if he could return to the mountain today. How have things changed in the intervening years and what does that mean for the future of mountaineering and Alpine climbing?

Everest Base Camp (EBC) is a very different scene now. Instead of a single, admittedly gargantuan, expedition each year, the Nepalese government now issues many permits and, at peak season, base camp is a sea of tents, people and too often rubbish left behind by climbers.

That’s quite sad and a far cry from what the 1953 expedition would have experienced, but so are the conditions and health of the Khumbu glacier which provides access to EBC and the start of the real climbing.

A recent study used declassified spy-satellite imagery to compare loss of ice mass across the Himalayas between the 1970s and the 2000s. They found that the rate of loss had doubled in the period 2000-2016 compared to the early epoch. They estimated the rate of thinning at the altitude of EBC was about 0.8 metres per year. The glacier is around 150 metres thick in the region below base camp. At the rate of thinning observed a decade ago it would lose about a third of its volume in 73 years exposing more and more loose and unstable rock.

However, my own work, with colleagues indicates that the acceleration in mass loss across the Himalaya has continued since 2016 to reach even higher rates. Google Earth imagery over the Khumbu glacier from 2021 shows extensive development of lakes on the ice surface: a sure sign of a glacier in decline. The lakes absorb more solar radiation than the surrounding ice and accelerate melt. There are, of course, no satellite images from 1953 but plenty of analogue photographs were taken and the changes are clear to see: now it’s more chaotic, more broken and more covered in debris.

The cause of the recent catastrophic flood event close to the Nepal/Tibet border has been linked to increasing regional temperatures, weakening permafrost (frozen ground that thaws with warming) and greater glacier melt rates.

In the European Alps the situation feels even more dire. In just two years from 2022-2023 glaciers in the Swiss Alps lost 10% of their volume. If that rate was sustained, they would be gone in 20 years time.

This year, mountain huts closed and guides stopped taking clients up the “normal” routes on the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc because it was too dangerous due to the high temperatures and the consequent increased rockfall.

Many other routes were being avoided because of the dangerous rockfall conditions. The first six months of 2026 were the third warmest on record and it is no wonder that glaciers, and the frozen world is responding to this level global heating .

In August 1990 I climbed perhaps the most iconic and well known route in the Alps: the north face of the Eiger. The photo below shows me on a section called the second icefield, a crucial part of the original 1938 route that gains you access to the upper face and the ominously named Death Bivouc. The icefield no longer exists, and no one who wants a relatively safe passage climbs the route in summer. The recommended climbing season now is late winter or early spring to avoid the rotten rock and dangerous conditions that summer brings. Thus, in my short mountaineering career, I have seen unprecedented changes on famous Alpine routes and a transforming landscape in the high mountains.

What does this mean for the future of mountaineering and glaciers? Based on current climate policies, the European Alps, western Canada and the US, Scandinavia and other regions are expected to lose about 90-100% of their mass by 2100.

That’s just 74 years away, roughly the time between that first ascent of Everest and now. It will have a dramatic impact on the mountain landscape, ecosystems, tourism, beauty and natural hazard exposure of these, once pristine, mountain environments.

EBC has not been beautiful or pristine for many years, perhaps less because of global heating and more to do with the reckless attitude of some of the expeditions that visit. I wonder what Tenzing would have made of the changes to both the landscape and attitudes that have occurred since his historic and heroic first ascent of Everest, the sacred “Goddess Mother of the World”?
Jonathan Bamber receives funding from the EC, the European Space Agency and Technical University Munich.

articles.title: How Jim Bakker became the Johnny Carson of Christian TV
articles.author: John Wigger, Professor of History, University of Missouri-Columbia
paras: When I was researching my 2017 book, “PTL: The Rise and Fall of Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker’s Evangelical Empire,” I interviewed dozens of former staffers and supporters of PTL, the ministry, television and theme park empire that the Bakkers built starting in the 1970s.
Time and again, I heard the same thing. PTL – sometimes known as “Praise the Lord” or “People That Love” – was both the best and worst thing they ever did.

The worst has been recounted at length, sometimes tinged with schadenfreude: the financial fraud, sex scandals, federal trials and prison time that plagued Jim Bakker, who died on Oct. 5, 2026, at age 86.

But it’s also worth remembering PTL as a pioneering force in Christian broadcasting. Working with a dedicated core of energetic young believers, Jim and his wife, Tammy Faye, built PTL from scratch, demonstrating how religion could be fused with pop culture and entertainment to better connect with American Christians.
From Billy Graham to Little Richard

The Bakkers had a talent for recognizing cultural trends and tailoring their message accordingly. In 1974 they launched their television show, “The PTL Club,” from a former furniture store in Charlotte, North Carolina. Jim’s vision was to create a Christian version of “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson,” then at the height of its cultural influence.

“The PTL Club” existed at the nexus of evangelical Christianity and American pop culture. Everyone who was anyone among evangelicals – preacher Billy Graham, gospel singer Pat Boone, fellow televangelist Oral Roberts – appeared on the show. But the Bakkers also booked unlikely celebrities, including singer Little Richard, Black Panther Eldridge Cleaver and Hustler magazine publisher Larry Flynt.
On any given episode, viewers might learn about passages from the Bible alongside candid discussions about sex, marriage, parenting, substance abuse, diet and exercise, and dealing with depression.

It could also be hilarious. During one show, Jim brought a camel on set that peed all over the stage. The charismatic and spontaneous Tammy Faye earned a reputation for speaking her mind, sometimes in off-color ways, that brought her legions of fans. When Tammy Faye did an episode entirely on a merry-go-round, one of the cast members vomited in the dog costume he was wearing.
In addition to introducing the Christian talk show format, PTL was at the forefront of pioneering satellite television alongside Pat Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network Satellite Service.

Satellite TV allowed television programming to be distributed across vast distances, bypassing the local broadcast stations and transmission infrastructure that had previously been needed to reach large audiences.

In 1978 – just three years after HBO began continuously transmitting via satellite and a year before ESPN went on the air – the Bakkers’ ministry started offering 24-hour Christian programming via the PTL Satellite Network.
The PTL network ended up reaching 14 million American homes, and its programs could be seen in 40 countries, turning Jim into an international celebrities and opening up new sources of fundraising.
‘God wants you to be rich’

In the “Greed is Good” atmosphere of the 1980s, Jim Bakker adopted what is often called the prosperity gospel: the Christian teaching that faith can bring material wealth, success and physical well-being.
“God wants you to be happy. God wants you to be rich. God wants you to prosper, even as your soul prospers,” he wrote in his 1980 book, “Eight Keys to Success.”

The Bakkers practiced what they preached. They used money earned from the PTL Satellite Network to buy a 10,000-square-foot (929-square-meter) home outside Charlotte and vacation homes in Florida; Palm Springs, California; and Gatlinburg, Tennessee. They purchased luxury cars, boats and finely tailored clothes. To many of Jim and Tammy’s supporters, this only proved that the prosperity gospel worked.

Had Bakker been satisfied with television, he might have still been at the helm of the PTL empire when he died. Instead, he used the television money to build Heritage USA, a theme park along the border of North and South Carolina. Long an admirer of Walt Disney, Bakker sought to build a Christian version of Disneyland.

Heritage USA was extravagant: It had a 500-room hotel, 5,000-seat television studio and US$13 million water park, along with a packed programming schedule of worship services, seminars, workshops, dinner theater and concerts.

But the enterprise cost far more than the television money could support. PTL was nearly always broke, leveraged to the point of collapse. As he struggled to keep the money flowing, Bakker fraudulently used funds raised for new projects to pay past debts.

On March 19, 1987, The Charlotte Observer published an article that described Bakker’s December 1980 sexual encounter with a then-21-year-old church secretary named Jessica Hahn in a Florida hotel room. Reporters detailed how PTL had paid Hahn and her representatives $265,000 in hush money. By then, PTL was $65 million in debt, losing $2 million per month, and on the verge of bankruptcy.
Bakker resigned from PTL in disgrace, and was sentenced to 45 years in prison for fraud in 1989. As Jim and Tammy Faye departed the courthouse, they sang the hymn “On Christ the Solid Rock I stand.”
The Bakkers divorced in 1992, while Jim was still serving his prison sentence. He ended up serving nearly five years before his release. Tammy Faye died in 2007.
Nearly everyone I interviewed for the book felt that PTL’s initial aim was pure: Spread the gospel to as many people as possible, using cutting edge technology.
But along the way, money and fame appeared to become the goal, not a means to an end.
